subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT

speechtext: Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Acting Prime Minister) moved that the house go into committee of supply.

subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Before the motion is carried, I have to deal with a most important matter. I read in one of the morning contemporaries that parliament should await Mr. King, and the editorial, after referring to reports that parliament may prorogue this week-end, goes on, "We don't think parliament should do anything of the sort", et cetera. It is an article appearing in the Ottawa Journal of to-day. I notice that the Prime Minister has given an interview to the effect that all his ministers should be here upon his arrival. When I look at the treasury benches and see many vacant seats, I realize that our cabinet ministers have become ambassadors of good will at large in various countries of the world. The Postmaster General is going to South America; another minister is away from Ottawa; the Minister of Agriculture is in Copenhagen, the Minister of Veterans Affairs has fled to Scotland to count the numbers of men who have not returned home, and the Prime Minister is at sea, as we are, while the Minister of Finance-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Speak for the Liberal party.

subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: I speak for the whole house at the present time in saying that. The Minister of Finance enjoys the scenery of Switzerland and looks at the paintings of Mr. Churchill over there.

subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Why don't you go
away?

subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Because it is my duty to be here. The Minister of Health is at the Paris conference and expects the translator to make him understand what is said there.

The ministers who are here deserve our sympathy to the utmost.

subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: We all deserve something right now.

subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: I will tell my hon. friend that if he interrupts me-[DOT]

subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: He will not be elected.

subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
-he will no longer be called the Jean-Frangois Pouliot of British Columbia and will run to defeat. By the way, it is always easy to heckle, but I have to speak of the sad position in which the House of Commons finds itself. It is not a matter for jokes. The other day when the members of the C.C.F. group were making their cases about labour matters I regretted very deeply that they were interrupted, because they are hard workers. I believe in freedom of speech, and when they have something to say they should be listened to. Those who do not want to listen to them have only to take the door or smoke outside the curtain. I say that in regard to all hecklers, because I certainly believe in freedom of speech, which is one of the guarantees of democracy in the country.
Now, sir, I wonder if this is what we call world government, to have the cabinet shelves empty and to have seats filled at UNO, UNRRA and all the other organizations of the world. For fifteen years I have suffered mental cruelty in the house.

subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
In this sense, that there is not one measure which has been sponsored by the government which has entirely satisfied my mind. Even when the purpose was good, the legislation was half-baked. This year we have enlarged bureaucratic control immensely by piling Ossa upon Pelion, meaning that we have piled reams of paper on top of reams of paper, legislation on legislation. It does not mean any replacement of bureaucracy; it means more bureaucracy than ever, and more bureaucracy means more taxation. I wonder whether there is one member of parliament who is satisfied with this session. Everybody wants to go home. I feel the same way as my colleagues, but I want to go home with some accomplishment of which the House of Commons will be proud. If we .go home and tell our constituents merely that the session has lasted from March until September, it will not satisfy them. If we tell them that we have passed legislation, such a quantity of legislation as was never passed before, they will say: What is the use? What the Canadian people want

The Ministry-Business oj Parliament
is order and good government. That is all they want. We cannot expect order in the country unless we have order within the government. To have order within the government we must have leadership. I say that with fervour and sincerity. I want ta be just as proud of the government of my country as I was from the first time I was elected until 1930. Since then there has been a great change. No longer do we have democratic rule in the country. We have irresponsible rule from outside. I wonder whether there will be any change in the method of government. if a change of government should occur some time in the future.
The last election took place in June of last year. Is there one member of parliament who is satisfied with the work that he has accomplished during the session? I do not say that to depreciate ray colleagues, whom I respect even when I disagree with them, and for whom I have admiration and sympathy; because the result which they achieve is far from the task which is imposed on them and from the sacrifices which they have to make to be true to the national duty of representing the people of Canada in the house.
It is unfortunate that so many ministers are away. It is most unfortunate because it puts a heavier burden on the shoulders of their colleagues who are acting ministers. In my view all the cabinet ministers, even those who are away, are able men. But I will tell you, sir, that in my view the House of Commons is a dense forest of cabinet timber-and not only within the ranks of the Liberal party, but also within the ranks of the official opposition and the other groups opposite. Members are not given the opportunity to show what they can do, because they are kept at work which keeps them very busy, which does not leave them the time or give them the opportunity to accomplish reforms which they desire to make in the public interest.
We have heard something about world government, world government for Canada. Are we for it? Is Canada to become a second Newfoundland to be looked after financially by those whom we have helped so much during the war? Sir, there was a pathetic moment in this house; when the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) left for overseas, that old gentleman, who has been in office longer than any other prime minister, was about to sail for Paris, who wished him godspeed? It was the leader of the official opposition; it was the leader of the C.C.F. group; it was the leader of the Social Credit group, but no one rose from this side of the house to extend greetings and good wishes to
him. I w'ent before the whole house to shake hands with him, to give him my personal good washes. It w'as not for me to rise after the leaders, to speak in the same vein and to the same effect, although my wishes were sincere.
I will tell you more than that, Mr. Speaker. At a gathering of the Liberal party after the Prime Minister had said he had made up his mind to leave, that it was definite and that he would not reconsider it, I waited for a few moments, and then as I saw that nobody rose to say a word of appreciation to him, I did so, as an old member of the house, an old supporter. of the party who had kept his independence intact and held it as a treasure. Those are facts. I find it pathetic that a man who has been the Santa Claus of so many people did not get a word of thanks from those who had been eating from his hand in the expectation of the fulfilment of some untold wish and desire; but, sir, that is human nature. There is a fact which is of the utmost importance. Nobody wished Mr. King to go; nobody dared to say that. We have too much respect and reverence for him. But Mr. King, as old man Simeon in his Nunc Dimittis, has said, "My task is completed. I desire to leave the leadership of the party to enjoy the last years of my life." A fair wish; a wish that is reasonable, because he has done his duty for so many years. His reward is obvious. He wants to enjoy the last years of his life in comfort and peace in his home, so as to meditate and write for the benefit of future generations.
Some people say Mr. King will have to stay in office, that we must await his return, and that parliament shall remain idle until he comes back. They say, "We must wait for him." I do not think Mr. King would agree with the editorial to which I referred just a moment ago. He is too big n man to think that he is more than parliament. How many times shall I have to repeat that parliament has power that reaches far above the government; because in my view, after having read authorities on constitutional law, the" government is not at all more than parliament. It is just a committee of parliament. Therefore, sir, it belongs to us, members of the House of Commons, to make suggestions in these difficult times so that the ship of state will get out of the fog, and so that we may have clear vision of what we have to do for the benefit of the Canadian people.
It is impossible to make any decision, because decisions are not made by some of those who adorn the treasury benches. Most of the
5502	COMMONS
The Ministry-Business oj Parliament
time decisions are made outside, by outsiders. Those decisions by outsiders are often to sabotage what has been done by those of us who are supposed to hold in our hands the destiny of this country.
Well, sir, I read a Canadian dispatch which appeared yesterday in all the papers.. It was a dispatch respecting an interview given by the Prime Minister before leaving for Canada, on his way home. Everybody has read it. I could easily refer to it, but hon. members will know what it is about. But is there anyone who will suggest that Mr. Mackenzie King's glory would not have shone more if he had resigned three months ago, before leaving for Europe? If he had done so, anybody could have gone to Paris. They would not have achieved, more success than Mr. King has achieved!. But everybody would have said, "Oh, if Mr. King had been there he would have had a branch of the olive tree in his hand to settle all difficulties and all differences. It is most unfortunate that Mr. King resigned so early. He should have been there."
As a supporter of Mr. King I want his glory to remain intact. That is precisely the reason I regret so much the pressure that has been put upon, him to prevent his doing what apparently he wanted to do, what the National Liberal Federation wanted to do immediately after the last election, in the summer of 1945, according to the statement made not long ago by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) when he said that the leadership of the Liberal party had been offered to him by someone of importance outside the house.

subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Who was that man?

subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: I do not know; I never heard about it. I never am consulted, any more than the hon. member is.

subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Nobody made any offer to, the leader of the C.C.F. party.

subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: I would take the word of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar just as much as I would the word of the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette). I respect them both.

subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
On a question of privilege, there has been mention inside and outside the house with respect to a man prominent in Liberal circles approaching the leader of the
C.C.F. party. No name has been given, and I should like to know what the name is. I believe the house is entitled to know that name, too.

subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
I remember that a former president of the National Liberal Federation

had said in Windsor a long time ago, before the election in 1935, that there was no difference between the C.C.F. and the Liberal party. And that is precisely why I was called by the party to Windsor to support the nomination of the late Hon. Norman McLarty, who later became secretary of state. I do not know whether it was the same gentleman who spoke to the leader of the C.C.F. group, because he was away when the conversation took place. But it could have been said by the National Liberal Federation, and it could have been said by Mr. Gordon Fogo, whom I object to as president of the liberal federation, because of his dealings with the Tories during the war. And, by the way, sir, I know my onions. When I state something I can give the evidence for what I am contending.
Well now, is it true that in this house-it is not necessary to go outside the house-there is no one who could slip into the shoes of the Prime Minister, when the duty of remaining leader of the house and Prime Minister against his own will is being imposed upon the present Prime Minister? I do not think so. I do not think it is fair to make a suggestion to the effect that Mr. King is the only man who can foe prime minister of Canada, after he has been prime minister for twenty years.
I repeat it is not a matter of disrespect, but rather one of urgency and of national importance. And if I had not spoken on this motion, sir, I am sure the house would have given its consent to debate the matter on a motion to adjourn the house to discuss a matter of urgent public importance, as this one is.
As I am proud of my colleagues, as I appreciate all of them, and as I appreciate the ungrateful task they are performing in the house, I want them to leave Ottawa not with a sour mouth but with content in their hearts and satisfaction in their minds. I would want them to go home with the conviction that we are contributing together to put the country on its feet for a better future for all Canadians.
The other day I listened to a moving speech by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) in which he said that party considerations did not affect him much. That is my position. I have been fighting for the Liberal party for a number of years because I expected reform. I have tried many ways to obtain reform, first by suggesting a union opposition composed of men of good will, before the three war ministers were out. Then I appealed to patriotism and to love of Canada, but without success. I appealed to liberal minded members of all parties of the house, leaving aside political

The Ministry-Business of Parliament
labels, ignoring them; I appealed to their sense of duty, which is another form of patriotism; now I make a special appeal to all true reformers.
The question is to obtain reform in the government; the question is to go back to the old democratic rule of responsible government; the question is not to use abstractions, to curse and denounce abstractions. We will get nowhere with that. It has been an honour for a long time to be the Prime Minister of this country; it was an honour when life was easier, when taxation was less, when there were no labour difficulties, when people earned less money but when money had more purchasing power. The people were contented and satisfied with their lot.
I remember having seen prime ministers of Canada in coaches driven by fine horses parading through our cities, which were all decorated, and making fine speeches that got great applause. Now conditions are different. Social life is of no importance for those who govern this country. We have evidence of that in the fact that prior to the war there were receptions that we do not have any longer. I do not complain about it; I understand very well that cabinet ministers do not have the time to entertain members of parliament as they did before the war. What is important is not to listen to fine, moving speeches made to large crowds on special occasions by the right hon. Prime Minister of this country and the hon. gentlemen who are his cabinet ministers, et cetera, et cetera; what we have to do is to roll up our sleeves and work.

subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Hear hear; let us get
at it.

subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Exactly. This is all the more so because last week in the senate committee I heard the governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Towers, declare that Canada can pay the tremendous debt we have-be seemed absorbed in his thoughts when he spoke those words-only with the sweat of our brow, with lots of luck and with plenty of time. Lots of luck provided that we come back to reality, provided that we put aside all dreamers, provided we give our confidence to men who have accomplished things, provided we give our confidence to realists and reformers.
I have never understood why in the world the Prime Minister holds so many portfolios. He is the Prime Minister of Canada, the first minister, which is the same thing. He is the President of the Privy Council. He is the Secretary of State for External Affairs. He is the leader of this house. It is an unusual
situation that the minister whom he appointed to replace him as leader of the house should have gone away while the house is still sitting. He is the President of the Privy Council, and the President of the Privy Council is far away from the east block at the present time.
In my humble view, and in the view of my constituents and of several English and French speaking Canadians, in these crucial times through which we are passing the Prime Minister should be only the Prime Minister. He would not .have enough time to head the Department of External Affairs. The foremost duty of the first minister of the land should be to supervise the departments and give them leadership and inspiration to rebuild and reconstruct this country. Is it impossible to find in this house a man who can fill that position in order to give the Prime Minister of Canada, whom I respect and whom I have defended, at times even against himself, a real rest when he has expressed so definitely his desire to get it?
It is the. privilege of a Prime Minister to choose his colleagues in his cabinet. I know that, and I knew it when I was rebuked by the Prime Minister after I had said that Tom Moore should not be minister of labour. I expressed that pious wish, and I was at once rebuked by the Prime Minister, who told me to mind my own business. In fact Tom Moore was not appointed minister of labour, and although I had received the rebuke I had the satisfaction of winning my point,
I admit it is the privilege of the Prime Minister to choose those with whom he wants to surround himself in the council room. That is his business, but it is the duty of the house to make suggestions so that the best choice is made of his successor, not by the Prime Minister but by the party as far as the leader of the party is concerned, and by the house in order to find a leader of the house. Government exists only as long as it has the support of this house.
After major consideration and thought I have come to a conclusion which I offer through you, Mr. Speaker, to the House of Commons. We are starting a new era. The war has been left behind and we are starting a real post-war and peace era. There are many ungrateful tasks, and I sympathize with the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) who has had to do things that were most unpleasant to him. But he did them from a sense of duty, he did them to be true to the dicta of his conscience and I admire him greatly for that. He enjoys the respect of all of us. When I think of all his colleagues I also have great admiration for them. Some of them are personal friends, and others
5501	COMMONS
The Ministry-Business of Parliament
deserve the consideration that they enjoy from all of us. I am sorry when I disagree with them on some matters. However, this is a free country and I appreciate the fact that I have never been canvassed in my office by any whip, by any minister or by any other Liberal member to change my views. The Liberal party is a party where freedom of thought is respected.
The war effort of: Canada was referred to by Mr. Churchill in New York during the war as being a massive effort. He said that in the presence of the Prime Minister. I cannot forget that the main artisan of the Canadian war effort, the man who organized war production in the country, was a man who worked day and night for his country. I know of no man in this house, and I say this with due respect to my colleagues whom I respect and admire, who could have achieved the miracle accomplished during the war by the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe). I have disagreed with him at times, especially in the early part of the war, but he and the able men whom he gathered around him deserved and got my admiration for the splendid task that they performed in those difficult times. In proportion to her population Canada has done more than any other country in the world for the war effort, and no one will say that the Minister of Reconstruction was not the main artisan of that magnificent and massive production.
The conclusion is obvious. The Prime Minister has said that he wants to go. It is absurd to force a gentleman who will reach his seventy-second birthday in a few months to stay at the helm of the ship of state any longer when he himself wants to go. I regret it, but that is his decision. But there is somebody to replace him, and I say this without deprecating the fine work done by all the colleagues of the Prime Minister. I think the man who should be in charge of reconstruction for peace should be the man w'ho was in charge of our war production. He is a realist; he has the finest possible background to accomplish that task. I suggest that he should be prime minister, but only prime minister to supervise the work of his colleagues whom he will be free to choose.
It is easy for any hon. member to "slate" a cabinet. All one has to do is to take a sheet of paper and put names on it. But it would be unjust. It pertains to the Prime Minister to make his own choice and come before the house and have the support of the house for his government. When I look around, I would not be surprised if some of the ablest men-and they are many-in the other groups would be invited to join in fMr. Pouliot.]
the formation of such a cabinet, which would be a real peace cabinet. How can anyone go to other countries and lecture them on what they should do when there is disorder in this country? The first duty of the Prime Minister is to stay here. The first duty of the Prime Minister is to his country. Mr. King has realized it, and now he is on his way back to Canada; and are we waiting for word from him to decide what we have to do? Therefore, sir, my suggestion is that the house should comply with the wishes expressed so often by the Prime Minister of Canada,-and this is for his own glory-

speechtext: What I am saying now is for the prompt expedition of the business of parliament. I have no other intention. We are all in the fog; we do not know where we are, and it is time to decide something. It is time to lose that inferiority complex which is the characteristic of fascist states, and we should come back to the democracy which is so often preached in this house when in fact it does not exist. As a Liberal, sir, I regret that when I defend the rights of democracy in this house, everyone who speaks his own mind, everyone who says aloud all that is said behind doors, is interrupted by those who have not the courage to speak out what they say in catimini.

But I will tell you, sir, that I hope those who have interrupted me, who call themselves Liberals but who are no more Liberals than they are Chinese, will be put out of the party in power and will be replaced by men of good will, by liberal-minded men coming from all other parties of the house; and the gain would be to the government' of the day. As a Liberal I am convinced, when I hear shouts and screams and howls and groans every time a member has the courage to stand up and express his convictions, that if we are in a democratic country, if the right of free speech exists, it is the duty of a man who has the faculty of saying what he thinks, to speak here what he believes is for the good of this country. subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
It is no pleasure to me to leave my part of the country to come here to-day and to take advantage of the last day on which I am afforded the opportunity to speak as I do now to say all I have to say to members of parliament, to complete what I have already said so often during the session, to inspire in them self-assurance so that they will be confident of themselves and can go back with pride to their constituents and say, "We have accomplished our duty; we have done our best to put the country in order."
The reason I mentioned the name of Mr. Howe is that his work has been sabotaged on housing and on aviation, and he has not been given full freedom of action to do what he wanted to do. Every time he has been prevented from doing what he wanted to do by those who think we can pay the tremendous
debt of this country by the sweat of our brow in lots of time and with lots of luck. Let us help ourselves now. The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply is in good health; he is not an old man; but I do not think that he will stay very long; it is a sacrifice which the country asks of him to require him to finish his job in order that he can organize peace. It is a great sacrifice and it will be a burden for him. I show that I have no narrowness of mind and no prejudice when I mention for such a high post one from whom I have differed at times but whose merit I recognize.
In all friendliness, sir, I thank very sincerely the house for the kind, reception they have given me. I hope some things will be done to comply with the wishes expressed by the Prime Minister, and that, without discrimination as regards any one of his colleagues, the house will choose a leader who is a realist, and who has accomplished so many important things in the past.
There will be young men who have legitimate ambitions, and after the country is again on its feet there will be opportunity for the party or for any organization to select a new leader. In the meantime we will have no elections, except under special circumstances, for a few years. The task of reconstruction must start now. It must not start in a month, in a year, in two years; it must start now, and be given a new impulse by a man who will have the supervision of all departments and who will have the authority to tell his cabinet colleagues what they shall do, each one as the head of his department, so as to perform the best possible task and enable us to achieve reform, not by speeches, but by example. I thank the house, sir, and I thank you.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee of supply, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.

subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Can the minister give some information about the preparations being made, in addition to those he mentioned last night, to receive refugees, of whom quite a number have applied for admittance into the
Supply-Immigration

country? In my riding there are two or three thousand Ukrainians, six or seven thousand Jewish people, four or five thousand Italians, perhaps two thousand Poles, and people of other European nationalities, as well as of course a large number of people of British origin. I have received from many of them, particularly from those originally from the continent, requests that last remaining relatives be allowed to come to Canada. In most cases, after inquiry I have sent the application on to the department. Some of these people who *would like last remaining relatives on the continent to come to Canada are comfortably off and able to take care of them, and they are ready to give any bonds required by the government so that the immigrants will not become a public charge.
I wish to support what the member for Spadina said last night. In my opinion, too, the time has come when we should follow the United States programme in preparing for an over-all immigration policy to see to it that folks of the best type are admitted, irrespective of race, ensuring of course that the predominant number will be from the British isles. To my own knowledge representatives of all the races I have mentioned, so far as my own riding is concerned, have done wonderfully well in helping to build up the country. I refer first to the Jews, the Ukrainians and the Poles. We have two Ukrainian members of parliament, one in the C.C.F. representing the constituency of Dauphin, and the hon. member for Vegreville; and we have one hon. member of Jewish race representing the constituency of Spadina. There may be others whose names I have overlooked. But certainly these three gentlemen, representing their races, have all demonstrated what this country owes to the people of their nationalities. The Italians, Poles, Russians and Scandinavians are also well represented in my riding. I concur in what the hon. member for Spadina said about the proposal to organize an over-all immigration plan, not forgetting that the predominant stock be British origin. I am in contact with organizations representing thousands of people of the nationalities to which I have referred, and I think that every effort should be made to allow the applicants to come in if they are fit and if and when they can be absorbed.

subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
In view of the remarks that have been made urging a greater degree of immigration, I think I should say a few words lest the impression be left that the house unanimously favours more immigration. I for one cannot subscribe to the policy, and

I wish to place on record my opposition to any opening of the doors until such time as we have set our own house in order.
In the first place, Canada has for years been the stepping stone for immigrants wishing to go to the United States. I have not had time to look up the figures, but I have seen them, and my recollection is that over a period of forty years. the national increase in population has been almost as large as if not larger than the number of immigrants who have left the country for the United States. This establishes clearly that a good many of these immigrants went to the United States or else drove some of our own Canadians to the United States. Just as phony money drives good money out of circulation, immigrants have been driving out the natives of this country. Statistics show that the proportion of Canadians of British descent is decreasing steadily and that of French extraction remains stationary. Is this situation healthy, or is it one that should be encouraged further?
While the majority of the people from continental Europe have proved to be fine citizens, particularly Ukrainians and Scandinavians, the fact remains that other groups have been a source of trouble at times. Before talking about bringing more people into the country we should look into our own labour situation. As the minister pointed out, we have yet to reestablish in civilian life a number of our servicemen, those actually in service and those taking vocational courses. Moreover, according to the report of the Minister of Labour, even at this favourable time of the year our unemployment is still quite high. Until this number is further reduced it would not be in the interests of labour to bring more labourers into Canada.
After all, the great majority of immigrants who have come to this country, including farm help and farmers, were manual labourers. All those in this house who champion the cause of labour must realize that labour is better served where unemployment is at the lowest ebb. For that reason immigration of labourers, except under special circumstances, cannot serve the cause of labour. Abundant labour always means a lower standard of living. In my humble opinion the only immigrants we might be able to absorb without too much danger at this time are farmers and would-be farmers.
Everyone realizes the importance of having this country thickly settled. There is only one way of doing that, and that is by occupying the greatest area of land and farming it. Merely increasing the population of the cities and towns would not in my opinion better

Supply-Immigration
our situation as a nation. If we wish to be a great nation we must occupy and cultivate more of our arable land. We shall not do this by bringing in industrial workers.
This may sound rather arbitrary, but I believe that in the best interest of Canada all unskilled immigrants should be admitted to the country on the understanding that they remain on the farm for at least one generation. The best way to develop love and devotion to a country and its institutions is to develop love and devotion to the land and the soil, and practically the only way to develop love and devotion to the land of the country is to clear that land and cultivate it.
I venture to say that all new Canadians who have spent the early years of their lives in this country in the pursuit of agriculture ,are far better citizens than those who have had to depend for their livelihood on other types of manual labour. Therefore our immigration policy should be directed towards bringing in people who are willing and anxious to till the soil. When this situation arises, to prove to the house that I am not opposed to immigrants of all types, I claim that we in the maritimes, and New Brunswick particularly, should have our proper share of immigrants. In my own riding there are hundreds of acres of good arable land, quite as arable and as valuable as the land in the western provinces. Let us have our share of farmer immigrants. We could settle thousands of them in my own riding, but I warn the government that what we need is farmers and not industrial workers, not pick and shovel immigrants.
Another reason why I consider immigration inadvisable is the housing situation, which is so serious. Where will you house the immigrants when you are unable to take care of your own people, your own veterans? I cannot understand the position of those who are clamouring for further immigration under present housing conditions. If deserving and desirable immigrants are anxious to come and ask us to receive them, then I think charity and justice bid us to receive them and treat them with the greatest degree of Christian kindness; but I see no reason for our making any special effort to bring people to this country unless they are anxious to come. If we do so we give them an implied undertaking that they will be pleased and well taken care of here. If they should be disappointed, they are apt to blame us for it.

subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
I do not propose to discuss the question of the whole immigration policy, because I believe the minister intimated yesterday that in a short time from now
it would be his mission to give to the house and to the country his view and the view of the government on the question of immigration as a whole. Therefore I shall confine my remarks to the question of the admitting of refugees and displaced persons.
Before I do that may I express my deep gratitude to the hon. member for Davenport for what he has said in his broad-minded way about the people of Ukrainian origin. I also express my gratitude to the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska. I do that because anything that I would say about the question of Ukrainian refugees or displaced persons can better be said by hon,. members who are not of Ukrainian origin. For that reason I want to place on record part of the report of the immigration and labour committee of the senate, which makes reference to the Ukrainian question. For obvious reasons I would rather have their opinion on record than my own views. May I say that this committee did a fine job in taking evidence both for and against the admission of immigrants into Canada. Therefore their report is based upon evidence taken on all sides of the question. First they make reference to other persons who are in displaced persons' camps, and then they have this to say about Ukrainians:
Ukrainians Available
There would appear to be at least an equal number of refugees and displaced persons of Ukrainian origin in the camps of Germany or drifting about Europe. Some millions of men and women were driven by the Germans from the territories they occupied to be used as slave labour. The home country of these people has been devastated, and it is thought that many would welcome an opportunity to recommence life in Canada. How suitable they are for settlement could be learned by careful investigations where they are, and by no other means. Our agents should be in Europe now engaged in this work, for if they are such people as the Ukrainian settlers who came to Canada in the years preceding the last war they will possess characteristics of _ intelligence and industry which may well contribute to Canada's development.
I place that on record because I would rather have the views of a body of men who took evidence from all sides, pro and con, and came to that conclusion, than place my own interpretation on it.
I should also like to make reference to another organization which appeared before the immigration and labour committee of the senate. I refer to the Canadian national committee on refugees, which was organized in 1938, the chairman of which is the Hon. Cairine Wilson, and the honorary chairman, Mr. B. K. Sandwell, two persons both well-known in Canadian life. After discussing the question of displaced persons and refugees
Supply-Immigration

before the committee they made, among other recommendations, this one which I consider to be most valuable in the immediate future. Their first recommendation was:
That Canada should state her policy on displaced persons immediately without waiting for decisions of the united nations.
They go on to say:
Australia has already made known her intention to take 70,000 immigrants annually. Great Britain, having accepted 150,000 to 200,000 oefore the end of the war, announced in the latter part of 1945 that relatives and concentration camp survivors would be admitted. The United States having taken about 250,000, has reopened quotas to provide for displaced persons of several nationalities and will admit a total of 39,000 a year.
They advocate that in proportion Canada do her share in admitting whatever number of refugees and displaced persons it is possible to admit in the immediate future. Another recommendation they make is as fallows:
That the important distinction be recognized between immigration policy and policy concerning refugees and displaced persons.
May I say that I found much with which I could agree when I listened to the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska, particularly when he said that at the present time it was not a question of opening the door wide to immigration until Canada's house is in order.
May I also refer to the attitude which organized labour may take? I wish to put on record what the Canadian Congress of Labour had to pay on this question on July 25, 1946. They recognized the distinction between imigration as a policy and the immediate policy of bringing displaced persons and refugees here to find a sanctuary. This is their fifth recommendation:
The admission of refugees, though it has, of course, economic aspects, is primarily a humanitarian question. Canada is under an obligation to humanity to admit her due share of refugees even if it costs her something. It may actually bring her important economic benefits. But even if it does not, she must do her part.
That is the view of organized labour, speaking as recently as July 25 of this year. It is a fair and humanitarian stand to take. Organized labour realizes that there is a danger in a period of mass unemployment, and in the housing crisis we are now experiencing overcrowding may work to the detriment of labour; but even in the face of that, from the point of view of helping people less fortunate than ourselves, organized labour is prepared to allow that class of people to come to Canada.

May I also refer to the recent convention of the National Council of Women, in which Mrs. R. T. Tanner, Toronto, who was the convener of the united nations committee of the National Council of Women, had this to say on June 6 of this year:
Approximately 750,000 persons in Europe cannot return home and must find new homes abroad. We must be willing to take a number of these unfortunate people and let the government know Canadian people are anxious to help solve this problem.
May I come back to another recommendation of the Canadian national committee on refugees. In their fifth point they recommend :
That immigration officers be sent immediately to the distress areas, particularly into the displaced persons camps.
The reason for that is obvious. In addition* to the shipping question, as the minister pointed out yesterday, there is the question of the inspection and selection right on the continent. I quite realize that the minister and the government want to be as careful as possible, and they should be, to see that the right type of person is admitted to Canada; that anyone who may bring jn some malignant disease, whether it be physical or mental, should not be permitted to come to Canada. I agree that great care should be taken. On the other hand there is definitely a question of urgency. We must remember that this problem of displaced persons and refugees arose even before the war ended. The war has now been over for a considerable period of time. Thees who are in the displaced persons camps have had the feeling that since the war is over, since conditions are more favourable, the allies will come to their rescue. The people are suffering, not only physically but mentally, because they are in a state of uncertainty; they do not know what is going to happen. They have looked to the United States and Canada as a sort of paradise to which they will be admitted when conditions permit. I feel strongly on this question. Perhaps because I am of Ukrainian origin I get more letters from people on this question than the average member would. But I know other members have received letters telling them of the desperate urgency of the situation. In fact I have received letters directly from overseas, from the displaced persons camps. I have taken pains to ascertain the truth of the allegations made in the letters, and I am satisfied that in respect of many of these people there is a degree of urgency which almost reaches desperation.
Let me make it clear that I am in favour of the government being very careful in

Supply-Immigration
checking anyone who applies for passage to this country, in that only those who will make good Canadians shall be admitted; but beyond that I doubt whether we should be too strict or too technical. Certainly we can no longer be dilatory. We should take as many of these people as it is possible for the country to absorb at this time, in order that they may get away from the conditions which surround them.

subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
I had not intended to say anything on this subject, but after listening with interest last night to the minister's statement I think something should be said now, because it may be too late when we meet next session.
One hon. member suggested giving a preference to European peasants rather than to English slum dwellers as immigrants. It just so happens there are thousands of city dwellers in England who would like to come to Canada.
Before proceeding further I should like to remind the house of what the English slum dweller has contributed to the welfare of democracy. It vTas slum dwellers in England who formed the first trade union in Great Britain. I refer to the Tolpuddle martyrs, who were slum dwellers and who were the originators of the trade union movement in Great Britain, a movement which has been supported loyally throughout the years by large numbers of people who would be termed slum dwellers. Those people have strong democratic instincts. I would say, too, that the foundation of the cooperative movement in Great Britain rests on the activities and support of the slum dwellers, as it was originated in the village of Rochdale. And that movement wras begun by what would be described as slum dwellers in what would be called now a slum. The cooperative movement in Great Britain has been built to a great extent by the activities and support and loyalty of the so-called slum dwellers of that country. It was built on the poverty and the pluck for which the slum dwellers in Great Britain are known.
Who first sensed the dangers of the fascist creed in Great Britain when some in high positions failed to realize it, and laughed Mosley's black-shirts into the backwaters of impotence? It was the slum dwellers of that country who did it. Who gave the world a greater example of heroism among a civilian population than the slum dwellers in the cities of England did during the last war? What civil population in the world's history has stood so fast and so firm, and under such difficult circumstances, and has defied tyranny, as the slum dwellers of England?
We owe them a debt of gratitude. If they had faltered at that time, if their morale had collapsed, history would be written in different terms to-day.
How many thousands of the troops on the beaches at Dunkirk came from the Slums of Great Britain? How many men in the eighth army came from the slums of Great Britain? How many men who came from those slums served in the British navy, air force and merchant marine?

subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: And in world war I, too.

subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Some people may question the advisability of bringing the so-called slum dwellers of Great Britain to Canada as immigrants. Anyone who knows Canadian history must know that thousands of them came to this country and have made an excellent contribution to its development. Hundreds of men in the public life of this country to-day, in different communities across the country, came from the slums of England. I mention these few facts because I want people fully to realize what contribution these humble people, who had so very little, have made to the development of democracy in Great Britain.	.
I am disturbed by the lack of immigration policy on the part of the government, and by statements which have been made. I was particularly disturbed when I read one of the reports of the senate committee on immigration, where a certain Lieutenant-Colonel Hicks, of Montreal, who until recently was a member of the Canadian portion of the military government in Germany, and who had under his control some twenty-two or twenty-three Canadian officers, suggested that we should admit four million Germans to this country as immigrants. Anyone who reads the record will see that. At the same time there are thousands in Great Britain who wish to come to Canada, but who are not getting any encouragement. I should like to tell the committee about an experience I had in the winter of 1938, just before the war. A young chap knocked at my door and asked lodging for the night. He was a young seaman from Glasgow who could not get employment in Great Britain. He had been on the dole for some years, and had heard that he could get employment on our great lakes as a seaman. He came to Canada, and after working two or three weeks on the great lakes on a pulpwood barge, the job was completed. Following that he hitchhiked across Canada, having been told that he could get a job on a ship in Vancouver. He travelled from Winnipeg to my home in the
Supply-Immigration

Kootenays, when, as I have said, that dark winter's night he knocked on my door, asking if I could put him up. I did so, keeping him for a week or so and in the meantime making arrangements for his transportation to Vancouver, where he thought a shipping job was available. The Canadian government deported that young man back to Glasgow. Throughout the years I corresponded with him because I was interested in what he was doing. The day war was declared he joined the merchant marine because a call had gone out for men to serve on the ships. He served throughout the war and was torpedoed several times.
Quite by accident, just before coming to Ottawa in March to attend the sitting of the house, I had the opportunity of speaking to him for ten or fifteen minutes in Vancouver. I said, "What do you intend to do when you get out of the merchant marine?" He said, "There is nothing I would like better than to come to British Columbia and stay on a piece of land." I might add that he was a hard-working chap, and capable. I said, "What have you done about it?" He said. "When we were in London I went to the office in that city, but I was given no encduragement whatsoever. I was practically told that they did not want any immigrants from Great Britain in Canada at the present time."

subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Imagine that!

subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
When we are discussing the matter of immigration I believe we must remember that, on the whole, Europe is short of man-power. Man-power is required throughout the devastated sections; but in Great Britain, with the exception of immediate reconstruction requirements, there will be a surplus of man-power.
I should like to read from a publication which quotes what a Mr. Wickman has to say. This man is a progressive British industrialist who was in Toronto some months ago. He said this:
"Canada is one of the millionaires of the new era. We in Britain, who were the pioneers of industrial development, are now one of the new poor. Britain's population is far above the ability of her domestic raw materials to supply."
Mr. Wickman advocated the transplanting of British industries to Canada with the transplanting geared to immigration. He left no doubt that if adequate labour were available, he would move his own vast enterprises to this country.
The hon. member who has just spoken said, I believe, that life on the land developed the greatest degree of loyalty and devotion to the country. I do not think any group of workers

could excel the industrial workers of Great Britain in the loyalty and devotion to democratic ideals they have shown in past years.
I realize that the question of displaced persons is a difficult one. I should like to pay tribute to all those of European stock who came to this country, and who assisted in its development and in our war effort. Many fine people have come to Canada from Europe; I have known many of them. But this is a question which causes many Canadians serious concern. There are some displaced persons in Europe who have suffered nazi tyranny and nazi oppression. Some of them want to come to this country, and we should admit them at the first possible opportunity. At the same time there are hundreds of thousands of displaced persons who helped Hitler until the day of allied victory. In this connection I should like to read from a letter written by a Canadian soldier and published in the Oshawa Times-Gazette, as follows:
Dear Sir:
I was very much surprised that there should be circles in Oshawa who would champion the right of Ukrainian quislings to receive asylum in this country. I refer to the item in your paper of November 27 which deals with a resolution adopted at the Ukrainian National Hall in regard to the so-called Ukrainian displaced persons now in Germany in the British and American zone.
I have first hand knowledge of these traitors since I met them in Upper Silesia while I was a prisoner of war. That is why I am not impressed about the claim that these people "are unable to return to their native land without endangering their lives on account of a system of terror practised by the Soviet government."
I ask you, Mr. Editor, what we Canadians would say about a number of our people joining the German army, fighting us and our allies and then seeking asylum in Russia on the grounds that we may want to try them for treason and therefore they should be protected from our justice?
These traitors should not be given asylum in Canada. I for one believe they should be returned to the Soviet authorities for trial.
I first came into contact with these Ukrainian quislings when I was shipped from Stalag No. 344, Lamsdorf to Bankau, Upper Silesia, in June, 1944.
I was in a working party of 24 Canadian prisoners of war who were engaged in forestry and sawmill work. This is how we came to know of the Ukrainian settlement nearby. The women used to work in the woods and their men would come to visit them on their leave. Our German guards told us they were Ukrainian volunteers in the German army. They wore the green-grey uniform of the Wehrmacht and acted like regular Germans. We often saw them when they came on leave.
There were other Ukrainians in Bankau. as well as Poles. Russians and other European nationalities. But these wore the tag of forced labourers and were treated as such.
You can well imagine how we Canadians felt about these Ukrainian volunteers in the German army. If we had an opportunity we would

Supply-Immigration
551.
have shot them there and then ourselves. We had more respect, if it could be called such, for our German guards as at least they were of the enemy.
Perhaps someone may ask: how come these people are now in the British and American zone? It's simple. They were afraid of the Red army and fled west into our lines figuring they can fool the allies with their anti-Soviet stories and claims that they were merely refugees from the terrible bolsheviki.
On January 18, 1945, our German guards began evacuating us westward into Germany because the red army was pressing the wehr-macht further and further west. The first to flee were these Ukrainian quislings. While we were forced to march hundreds of miles on foot they grabbed every vehicle in sight to get out of the way of the red army. We met hundreds of them, a disorderly mob, scared for their skins. Their objective was the American and British lines.
Now these same people have -got in touch with their friends in Canada and want to be brought here to continue their dirty work. As an ex-prisoner of war I thought I would give the citizens of Oshawa an. idea just who are these alleged displaced Ukrainians. They do not deserve our sympathy. They are traitors to the Ukraine, our ally and should be shunned as such. Certainly we should not put a premium on treachery.
The honest, patriotic Ukrainians, Russians and Poles and others who were forced labourers or prisoners of war are back home in their own countries. It is only the quislings who are afraid to face their own people, who are left in the American and British zones. I say, return them to their country to face the music there. They deserve no better.
Yours truly,
George Metcalfe.
I am not suggesting that all displaced persons are of that type, but it should put us on our guard in the selection of immigrants. If we want to have a satisfactory immigration policy we should first do more to retain in Canada those Canadians who have been trained at Canadian expense. We are losing hundreds of our choicest men to the United States because of a lack of opportunity in this country for their particular type of trained minds and brains.
We should welcome all those British people who fought the battle of Britain, those who fought in the army, the air force and the navy of Great Britain, or of any country in the commonwealth, and their relatives; those who defended our freedom and our opportunities should be welcomed. At the present time we are providing transportation for 4.000 Poles, and I understand we are to provide transportation for 6,000 displaced persons. It is hardly enough to say that British people can come to Canada provided that they get transportation. The fact is they are not in a preferred position. I have had numbers of [DOT]letters from people in the old country who are
anxious to come to Canada. There is no doubt that our offices in England are not giving encouragement to these people.
First, we should make arrangements for the transportation of people of British stock who want to come to this country. Second, we should give every consideration to the refugees of Europe-and by these I mean those people who were proved to be opposed to nazism and fascism, people who have suffered because of their loyalty to democracy. No group in Europe has been proven to be more completely anti-nazi than the Jewish race. These people have suffered terrific trials throughout the years and they should be given every consideration.
This is a problem that should receive the serious consideration of the government. We need immigrants in Canada, but we should have selective immigration. We must not forget that we have displaced veterans and displaced industrial workers in Canada, and we should have a policy which will permit us to absorb those people as fast as we can without disturbing our national economy. By adopting a policy which will make certain that only people of democratic faith shall be permitted to come to this country we shall be basing our future on sound foundations.

subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: May I ask the member one simple question: Would he say that the people whom he refers to as being anti-nazi were also anti-communist ?

subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: I am not a communist, and in fact with my views I think I would be considered a poor candidate for membership in the communist party. We must remember that these people fought against Hitler; they fought against fascism and nazism. Those were the terrors to mankind, and they still threaten mankind to-day, but they will not wish to come.

subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
I think there are two things we should seek to avoid in discussing this matter of immigration. First, we should avoid dealing with it on an emotional basis. Second, we should avoid any effort to bring immigrants into this country on the basis that prevailed for so many years in this country when people were brought here only for the purpose of being exploited. I think it was a predecessor of the Minister of Mines and Resources, who held office when the department was known as the Department of the Interior, who said that the kind of immigrant we wanted in Canada was a sturdy peasant in a sheepskin coat with a stout wife and half a dozen children. He said we wanted people who were accustomed to working on
Supply-Immigration

the land, who all their lives had worked from dawn until dark, who did not know anything else and who did not expect anything else. We do not want immigration based on that kind of philosophy. We want the people who come to Canada to have ideas as well as the ability to work and produce.
It was stated this morning that we should not bring anyone here until we had provided for our own people, until we had made our own people secure. That would be a good position to take if we had worked out a policy to take care of our people. Ouir people will remain in insecurity, poverty and misery whether or not other people are brought in, unless we have some planned policy for developing our resources. In my opinion that is not a very strong position to take. It was said that the standard of living of workers is always at its lowest when we have large numbers of people looking for work. True, but that applies not only to thickly populated countries but to countries with sparse populations, as we learned to our sorrow during the depression years. It will always apply as long as labour is regarded as a commodity, as long as working people are mere packets of labour power looking for a purchaser. We are not going to overcome that difficulty simply by keeping people out of the country and to that extent preventing its development.
Then the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska said that we should bring into this country only those who could be put on the land. But our farmers will continue to have difficulties in disposing of their produce if we do not organize our production and marketing. The only essential difference between the economic position of the farmer and the industrial worker is that the industrial worker sells his labour direct to an employer for a price, wages, while the farmer turns his labour into certain commodities, depending upon the particular type of agricultural production he is engaged in, after which he is in the same position as the industrial worker, that is, he must find a buyer for his commodity. As long as that condition prevails both the farmer and the industrial worker will be insecure, not because there is a scarcity of the things they need but because there is an over-abundance. What we have to do first is to organize our economy on a basis whereby the people will be prosperous when we have an abundance and not quite so prosperous when we have shortages. It is with that understanding that we should approach these questions.
It was said that an immigrant coming into this country should be compelled to remain

on the land for a generation in order that he might learn to love the land. That is a fallacious argument, and we will realize that if we will only observe that our land is being denuded to-day by people who have owned it and tilled it for several generations. They are leaving the land, not because they do not love the land but because the organization of our economy is such that they are not able to make a living on the land. These problems all have to be solved, and they are not going to be made any easier or any harder of solution because a few immigrants are allowed to come into the country from parts of the world where their circumstances are worse than ours.
The hon. member for Dauphin in opening his remarks said that he was a Canadian of Ukrainian extraction. I am not particular what his national origin is; the sentiments he expressed to-day are those of a Canadian, and as such they are good enough for me, who because of aqcident happen to be Canadian born. I am sorry I was not in the house last night when the minister spoke, but I would impress upon him, though perhaps it is unnecessary, that we in Canada have an obligation to people in other parts of the world where conditions are hard. We should be careful and selective in choosing those who are to come, because it is a high honour to be accorded the privilege of Canadian citizenship. But we should not be so careful that we keep out worthy people in order to exclude those who are unworthy, is has already been said by a number of speaktrs, there are people who because of their necessity are not in a position to wait, and special provision should be made in cases of that kind.
We should have an immigration policy which would enable people to come to this country-and in this I agree with the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska-who are anxious to come here, and we should do everything possible to see that they are properly settled and are not brought here for exploitation, as has been so often the case in the past, and that in the process of settling them here we may also put our own domestic affairs in order.

subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. POULIOT-THE MINISTRY- BUSINESS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
I was very much interested in the speech of the hon. member for Kootenay West and1 his support of the industrial workers of Great Britain. It should not be forgotten by any of us who hail from the prairie provinces that perhaps the greatest contribution to agriculture which was ever made in the prairie provinces was made by a man who spent the first forty years of his life in the city of London. He migrated to Canada to become a farmer, and made such a success of it that he is regarded as a dis-

Supply-Immigration
tinguished agriculturist. Though he had no academic training, he is one of the greatest authorities on agriculture in western Canada: I refer to Doctor Seager Wheeler. I learned also just the other day in my constituency that one of our most substantial farmers was born and raised in the city of London and is a nephew of a former lord mayor of London. I just mention these things to indicate what I believe to be the resourcefulness of the British industrial worker: he acquits himself admirably in any situation which he may be called upon to face in this country.
But my purpose in rising was to support particularly the stand of the hon. member for Dauphin, who was championing the cause of the displaced persons or refugees who find themselves in. a very serious position, in western Europe particularly. They are located in Germany, for the most part, in some areas in France, in Belgium and in Holland. Most of them were forced out of their homes through fear of persecution, religious or otherwise, and found themselves in these locations at the end of hostilities. They have made the best of their very difficult situation by living in barracks which they constructed out of any makeshift materials. Those of us who were fortunate enough to visit Great Britain last December and were able to go to the continent, including the hon. member for Peel, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, and myself, had the opportunity of visiting some of these displaced persons' camps in the vicinity of Oldenburg, in Germany, and our opinion was that they are just about the very best of immigrant material that Canada could want to have. We did not see them all, of course. They are scattered pretty well all over allied-occupied' Germany. How many there are is a question; I doubt if there are any accurate statistics regarding the number; but the Christian Science Monitor, which has good sources of information, has placed the number at approximately one and two-thirds million. Most of these people come from Poland, Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, and many of them, from south of there, who are known as Ukrainians. They are of course unable to come to Canada at the present time, and they expressed themselves to us as being desirous of coming here rather than to any other country. I should like to place on the record the opinion of a very important body of people in this country. I quote from United, Nations News, June number, a publication printed in Ottawa by the United Nations Society in Canada: one short resolution is as follows:
U.N. Society supports . . . more liberal immigration policy . . .
"Whereas there are many people throughout the world, particularly in Europe, whose lives have been disrupted by the war and who wish to make a new life for themselves, and whereas many of these people could make a valuable contribution to the life of Canada: t Therefore, be it resolved that the United Nations Society in Canada urges the government to initiate a programme of selective immigration which will permit immigrants to come to Canada in greater numbers and under more liberal conditions than was possible before the war."
I emphasize the last part of that sentence. I should also like to refer to a publication called the International Journal, which is published by the Canadian Institute of International Affairs. The spring number of 1946 contains an article entitled "Parallels in Soviet and Canadian Settlement." I do not intend to quote from this article, which is quite long. It describes the two countries and points out that, whereas Russia has at least twice as large an area as Canada, her population, at least as regards the rehabilitation of Siberia, has been going up by leaps and bounds as compared with ours. A synopsis of this article has been made by the financial editor of the Toronto Globe and Mail, May 9, 1946. I quote from it in part as follows:
The dominion covers 3*7 million square miles, the Soviets control over 8 million. There are 170 millions in the Soviet and only .12 million Canadians. The Soviets speak with assurance of a population of 340 million people and some Canadians talk as though 12 million is a good place to stop.
Although this article does not directly assert this conclusion, the inference is that it would be dangerous for any country in the world to-day to tolerate a vacuum, and also an inference which I, at any rate, read into it, that if we do not fill the vacuum by our own volition, somebody else may fill it for us some day to suit themselves and not to suit us. Therefore I am very glad to support the argument of the hon. member for Dauphin; for I believe that in Europe we now have the last potential reservoir of good citizens, or the making of good citizens, who should be brought to Canada in large numbers. I am not arguing that we could take them all, because a great many of them will be unfit for colonists anywhere. Possibly through health or age or infirmity, many of them will never be taken out except in a spirit of tolerance or more or less for humanitarian reasons.
The minister said last night there would be a division of these among the various countries who would be obliged to relieve the congestion; nevertheless that would be a very small part of our obligation and it would be far outweighed by the good results we would

There are very few Ukrainian settlers in my part of the province, but the population of Manitoba is over ten per cent Ukrainian in origin, and we have no better citizens. I am not saying this to gain any personal support because there would be none coming to me in my own area; but I know many, among them school inspectors, from our district, who have been working among the Ukrainians and they will vouch for it that there are no better citizens to be found anywhere in western Canada than the Ukrainians.
