subtopic: COMMA'S
speechtext:
Last night the minister made a remark regarding the four thousand Polish soldiers who are being considered as possible immigrants into Canada. I think the house would be remiss in its duty if it did not probe into the matter of the Poles with some care, because we may be getting ourselves into difficulties we might be sorry for if all should not be found as well as it might appear to be. At page 5495 of Hansard the minister said:
In addition to that, there are 4,000 Polish soldiers, the investigating officers for which are now on their way. I believe they are now in Italy making investigations with regard to these Polish soldiers to bring them to this country. They will be apportioned throughout the Dominion of Canada, according to the regula- * tions laid down by the Department of Labour.
I asked the minister this question:
Will the minister say why these Polish soldiers were admitted?
I have gathered since that they have not yet been admitted, and I hope they have not. The minister then replied:
The reason was that we were making an effort to take in soldiers who would go on the land, and into agricultural pursuits. We had many requests, and there was quite an agitation with regard to the Polish soldiers. They had expressed their intention most freely, that they were not going back to Poland, and that they intended to look elsewhere. Canada was one of the places to which they would go.
Our soldiers and their dependents were the first obligation we had.
I might have been a little over-suspicious, but something about the words the minister used troubled me at the time and it has been troubling me more ever since. Therefore I would like to find out more about the mean-ning of some of the expressions he used. I am going to ask him a series of questions to which I would like to get answers. If he can give them now, so much the better; if not he can give them later. I think the dominion [Mr. Wmkler.l
as a whole is entitled to have an answer to every one of these questions and to have it in the minutest and most sincere detail.
The minister spoke of the soldiers going on the land. Have we put on the land all our own soldiers who would go on the land? Have the soldiers from Holland, Denmark, Roumania and the Ukraine sought admittance to Canada, and has their request been considered as sympathetically as the request of the Polish soldiers?
May I make this comment at this point

the member for Vancouver East was, I thought, on that line of thought. Canada had a surplus of agricultural products before the war. What assurance have we that we shall not have a surplus of meat, grain, dairy products, fruits,, et cetera early in, the postwar years? Is it proposed to have these Poles displace Canadian farmers?
Let me pause here for a moment to comment. It has been my observation that many times people have been brought in from European countries and placed in good Canadian communities to help in various agricultural activities. They have remained there probably fifteen years and have then begun to buy out the original Canadians who had good British names, and in whole areas of the country you can hardly find a name like Smith or Brown or Jones or McNab. They are all some sort of un-British name now. I am not reflecting on any nationality, but I am not sure the tendency I refer to is in the best interests of Canada as a whole. I think that matter should be carefully assessed. Perhaps . the minister cannot reply to these comments, but I should think he would be able to answer some of the questions I am going to ask.
"Quite an agitation", he said, was being conducted in respect of the Poles. I believe the house is entitled to know who were the people who were agitating. Was it the Polish soldiers themselves? Was it the Polish government in exile? Were there any organized groups outside Canada or were there any organized groups inside Canada? I trust I can ask the questions I am going to ask without offending anyone. We have to face facts exactly as they are, and ask questions even if they do hurt. Was the agitation by any provincial government in Canada? Was it by any labour organization? Was it by any industrial organization? Was it by any political organization? Was it by any religious organization? Was it by any political leader or any religious leader? The facts are probably government secrets, but I believe

Supply-Immigration
every person in the dominion to-day is entitled to know exactly who the people were who were conducting the agitation, and I believe the members of the house have a solemn duty to find out before many more hours pass.
I have also this question to ask: What are the political affiliations or predilections of these Polish soldiers? That matter has already been referred to to some extent. Were they fascists when in Poland? I gather from some of the remarks I have heard that these people were not welcome in Russia. Why? And if they were not welcome there, what might be the reason why they should be particularly welcome in Canada? Were they fascist or communist or liberal? Were they monarchists or totalitarians or democrats? What is the record of each of these soldiers?
I know there are four thousand, but if it is expected to bring them all here, these questions should be asked with narrow scrutiny and the answers recorded. We have about all the troubles in Canada that we can take care of right now; let us see to it that we do not bring agents here who will aggravate those troubles. I want to see Canada a home for all honourable people and people of good will who will become worthy Canadians, but I am not at all in favour of bringing in people who will become agitators from the day they set foot on our shores-and we have too many of that type right now.
I want to know what are the religious affiliations of these Polish soldiers. Are they Protestant, atheistic, Roman Catholic or Judaistic? I do not want to do anything I ought not to do but I believe every member of the house realizes that any preponderance of any one of these among new immigrants would certainly be creating a handicap to large bodies of the Canadian people.
We have to face these facts realistically, and in particular with reference to these Poles-and may I just stop for a minute to refer to all the members that the hon. member for Lisgar was referring to. I sympathize with the fine ideals which were expressed in the quotations which the hon. member read. Nevertheless I tell the committee that we have all the internationalists that we want in the country right now; we have all the centralizers and general stargazers that we need. I do not want a whole lot of others in here. Of course, now it is popular to go clean crazy over internationalism, but by and by, unless we are careful, we shall wake up from the honeymoon phantasy we are in and begin to realize that in being too international we made a colossal mistake.
I should like to know what are the religious affiliations of these men. Are they evenly divided in the proportion that the major religions are divided in Canada? If it should be found that these men all belong to one religion, no matter what religion that is, I do not think that, taking them as a whole, it would be the will of the Canadian people that they be admitted.
In what provinces are the Polish soldiers to be settled? Has each province concerned been asked its consent? I do not wish to comment too much on that, but already we have groups in this country who were located by shortsighted governments in Ottawa and were placed on the lap of certain provinces. Those provinces are even yet not sure that they are going to be able to get rid of the problem so created. I see very serious complications. It is easy enough to get people in and plant them on the doorstep of the province and wash your hands of the problem. That simply is not good enough.
Is it proposed to settle these Polish soldiers in a block, or community? What are the "regulations laid down by the Department of Labour" under which these people will be settled? In my judgment every hon. member is responsible for speaking to the house in accordance with the experiences which he has had. That is how we make a contribution to each other. I have had unfortunate experiences with groups of people who settled in communities and cannot be changed into Canadians, who insist on keeping their own language and culture and going on from generation to generation. That is not good. If people are to be good Canadians they must be ready to assimilate in this country. The settling of groups in blocks is not conducive to that laudable objective. That ought to be definitely understood.
Where is it proposed to settle these soldiers? Are these proposed soldiers already in Canada? I gather from a rereading of the minister's words that they are not, and I am glad they are not, because we can still deal with the situation without being too severe. Where are they? Why all the haste about bringing them in? I understand that there was an order in council passed to admit
4,000	Polish soldiers. That seems to be an astounding thing. Why should there be such desperate haste that an order in council had to be passed to admit 4,000 Polish soldiers? Was it because the soldiers are suffering? Well, there are hundreds of thousands of other suffering people in Europe. Try to get one of these people into the country and see what happens. Every hon. member knows that you cannot get one of them in. You cannot even get a budge in the department of immi-
Supply-Immigration

gration; no, sir. I am not saying that is not as it should be, but what astonishes me is that we should pass an order in council, if that is what was done, to permit the entry of 4.000 soldiers because they are suffering! If that was not the reason for consenting to admit them, what was the reason? Why were they not going back to Poland? We can have whatever attitude towards Russia we wish, but when a body of people 4,000 strong are undesirable in their own homeland under Russian control and they seek admission to ours, we owe it to ourselves as a great duty to know something about the reasons why they were not going back to Poland.
The minister used these words: "Our soldiers and their dependents were the first obligation we had." That sounds innocent enough until you begin to think about it. "Our soldiers"; were these 4,000 Polish soldiers our soldiers? If they are classified as such what claim have they to be classified as our soldiers?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. GLEN (Minister of Mines and Resources):
subtopic: COMMA'S
speechtext:
Dealing only with the question of the 4,000 Polish soldiers, the hon. gentleman expressed a good deal of suspicion of the word "agitation" which I used last night. He seemed to imply from the word that there was a good deal of lobbying going on regarding the admission of these soldiers. Let me hasten to assure the hon. member that there is no such thing as lobbying in connection with this matter at all. He knows as well as all of us know that there are 200,000 Polish soldiers who fought with our armies and who were fighting against nazism about which the hon. member spoke. He knows that the soldiers cannot return to their home for the very reason that they have fought against nazism, and in effect they are to-day stateless.
The hon. gentleman wants to know what religious denomination they are. I personally will say that I will not inquire as to the religious denomination of any immigrant who wants to come to Canada provided he is a citizen worthy to be received into the country. When these officers go that is one of the questions that will not be asked, whether they are of a certain religious persuasion. There is no discrimination against any immigrant coming into Canada on the basis of his religion, and there has not been from any time back. The agitation for their admission to Canada, if that word is to be used, came from all over the world.
In every editorial of every newspaper in Canada one read accounts of the hardships being endured by these Polish soldiers, and the need that something should be done in

order if possible to rectify their condition. There were 200,000 of them; and the dominion government, without any special references I know of from any particular body, but following the general opinion of the country, decided that it would make that contribution to the relief of -these soldiers.
Our officers are going over there. I did not know, personally, any of those officers, but when I was informed as to the gentleman who was heading them I found he was a personal friend of mine. I did not know that, however, until he had been appointed. He was attached to the Department of Agriculture. This matter is more in the hands of the Department of Labour than in the immigration branch. However, I would say that our branch will attend to the landing of these soldiers when they come. The department has given careful consideration to those very matters about which the hon. member has spoken. I do not know whether the hon. member is aware of the fact that all those who come will be single persons, and that there is no question as to families coming.
Perhaps the Minister of Labour can deal with this matter in more detail than I can, but I believe the same process will be adopted as was adopted by the provinces with regard to the supply of labour for harvest. The provinces will be consulted. These people will be placed on individual farms, not with any intention of having them form a block, as was suggested by the hon. member-because that is not the intention at all. They will be placed on individual farms, and in that way will make their contribution. After a period of two years, if they prove to be acceptable as citizens they will be given their landings in Canada, with a view to becoming Canadian citizens under our new a'ct. There is nothing of a sinister nature behind it at all; there is only the desire of the government to make its contribution to what was a grievous situation so far as these soldiers were concerned. In respect of farm labour, let me say that I have heard it stated time and again in the house that there is not sufficient labour on the farms. These men are 63260-347
being chosen as farm labourers. The hon. member asked if they would be put into blocks in connection with the purchasing of farms. The government has no such intention. In the very nature of things, with 4,000 people spread over the Dominion of Canada, it must be clear that there is no purpose in putting them into blocks, because that would not be advantageous to individual farmers in Canada. They will be spread over the country, in the manner that the Department of Labour deals with the provinces and will be apportioned accordingly.

Hon. members have stressed the importance of selecting immigrants for Canada. I am wondering what tests are to be applied to immigrants. It used to be simple. The immigrants were selected on their physical condition, with perhaps some regard for their financial position. If they had a little money it was all to the good. However, the physical condition was the chief consideration. That is not true to-day. Physical condition should be neither the only nor the chief test. It is the mental and moral condition of immigrants that should be examined. Why are so many people anxious to come to Canada to make their living and to spend their lives here? Why are they so anxious to leave countries which physically are just as desirable, and some of them more desirable as a place of residence, than is Canada? Is it for material reasons that these people desire to come to and live in Canada? No! They seek the individual freedom which the people of Canada still enjoy, but which has been destroyed in the greater part of Europe. It is that freedom which we enjoy in Canada that must be guarded at all costs.
The minister has said it was not the purpose of the department to inquire into a person's religion. That may. be so. But to-day if we are to safeguard the freedom of the Canadian people, it is necessary to inquire into the political affiliations of immigrants wishing to come to this country. There can be no doubt that those countries of which Canada is one, which have thus far preserved the freedom of individuals, have become the mecca of all peoples who now exist where freedom has been lost. The very reason for our freedom is this:	So far Canada has
resisted the disruptive poisons of Marxian

socialism which destroyed the freedom of the people of Europe and brought about the terrible calamities which have overtaken that continent. Perhaps the minister will be able to tell the committee by what means they will test the mental and moral fitness of those who want to come to Canada. Personally I do not know how it can be done especially in these days of turmoil when it is almost impossible to find out just what a person does stand for.
I should like to say one word on behalf of these Polish soldiers. It seems to me that they have qualified for entry. When I was in England I was told on all sides that no one had fought more gallantly against the nazis than these Poles. That rules out any possibility of their being fascists or nazis. Since they are not welcomed in any country controlled by Russia, that rules out the probability of their being communists. It would seem to me that being neither one nor the other they should become good supporters of the Canadian way of life, which is neither socialist, nor communistic nor fascist.
One magazine-I do not know how large a circulation it has-is opposing the entry of these Poles because they are Roman Catholics. I think I am right in saying that of necessity any Christian in Poland would be a Roman Catholic because that is the religion of the country. I have no religious prejudice at all. I am not a Roman Catholic, but just the same I believe that Catholicism is one of the safeguards against communism and nazism. I sincerely hope it is, anyway.
That is all I wanted to say. I do not know whether it is possible for the minister to tell us how the suitability of these immigrants is to be decided. Physically it is a simple thing, but when you come to philosophic reasons it would seem to be a most difficult thing to determine. I want to impress upon the government the necessity of taking every precaution against the entry of those imbued with ideas contrary to the Canadian spirit which has made Canada the mecca for the free. I refer to our personal freedom of the individual.

MR. SINCLAIR (VANCOUVER NORTH)-SERVICE OF CANADIANS IN AFRICA UNDER FIELD MARSHAL MONTGOMERY

I should like to rise to a very personal and friendly point of privilege. Hon. members of this house object occasionally to what is said in this house, and also to what is said in the press of this country. To-day I wish to make a correction, not of what has been said in this house, or of what has been said in the press of this country, but of what was said on parliament hill to-day by, I think, the greatest soldier this war has seen, the soldiers' soldier, Field Marshal Viscount Montgomery of Alamein. It was a pleasure to hear him, but there was one special remark he made to which I have to take, on behalf of my own comrades, a personal objection, when he said that he had led Canadians everywhere except in Africa; because I should like in this house to remind the Field Marshal and to remind this house that, as Commander of the Eighth Army he led the desert air force, in which over five thousand Canadian aircrew served, and which, before Field Marshal Montgomery got to the desert, was led by the greatest Canadian airman who ever took wing, Air Vice-Marshal Raymond Collishaw, and in which desert air force, after Field Marshal Montgomery took command, there was one 63260-3471
all-Canadian squadron, the City of Windsor squadron, of which I was a very humble member.
More than that, before I sit down I should like to pay a personal tribute to one of the staff of this House of Commons. As I stood in my office, which fortunately fronts on parliament hill, and listened to our excellent Royal Canadian Mounted Police band play tunes of the last war, and tunes which I did not recognize, it occurred to me that these bands are missing one thing; because for Field Marshal Montgomery of Alamein one piece should have been played. The ceremony ended, and our carillonneur of the peace tower here, who is, I am glad to say, a former airman, played the one piece of the desert, the piece of the Luftwaffe and the Afrika Ivorps, the piece of the Eighth Army and the desert air force, "Lili Marlene."
I hope that Field Marshal Montgomery will accept this correction, for there were a great many Canadians who did fight very gallantly in the desert.

Hon. II. F. G. BRIDGES (Minister of Fisheries): Mr. Chairman, in presenting the estimates for the Department of Fisheries for this year, it is not my intention to make any prolonged or extended remarks, but there are some observations regarding the reorganization and expansion of the department which I feel I should make at this time.
When speaking before the committee of the whole house on my estimates, December 17 last, I made the following statement;
No doubt the future will entail certain expansion and changes in the department. I cannot go into detail at this time but we have hopes of producing adequate staff of high calibre and properly trained. In this connection I might mention that we shall be looking for recruits from among those of our young men who have been in the three armed services and who are now returning from overseas. These new recruits will be given proper courses of instruction which, it is hoped, will make them educationists as well as police officers.
I am pleased now to be able to report to the committee that, in so far as the outside administrative service of this department is concerned, those plans have now become crystallized and steps are now being taken to bring 100 new fisheries inspectors into the field service on the east and west coasts. A basic feature of this plan is an arrangement under which a group of applicants on each
Supply-Fisheries

coast will undergo a period of probationary training carried on under the joint auspices of the Department of Fisheries, the Department of Veterans Affairs and the vocational training branch of the Department of Labour. Thirty-five appointments to inspectorships are to be made in British Columbia; and in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, where our problems are different and local conditions necessitate a greater enlargement of field force there will be sixty-five all told new inspectors appointed, making the total of 100 for both coasts.
Increase in our inspectorship strength in British Columbia and the maritimes has been made necessary by the increase which has taken place in recent years in departmental functions and by changes in their nature and scope. In order that we may serve present-day needs of the fishing industry as effectively as possible and assist in further fisheries development, the department must have additional field officers, and we are setting out to get them from among men who not only show natural qualifications for this sort of work, but have also been specially trained for the job.
The core of our recruitment scheme is in this arrangement to obtain the new officers from among people who have satisfactorily completed specific probationary training. I am told that we are breaking new ground in requiring applicants for positions in the public service to qualify for appointment by taking prescribed training under departmental control, but I do not think there is any question that it is a sound move.
In this connection, only applicants approved by the Department of Veterans Affairs for grants, which it provides for ex-servicemen completing their education or undergoing training, will be considered for these new inspectorships. Preference will be given to applicants not more than thirty-five years old when applications close, but exceptions may be made in the case of men not over forty years of age who are considered to possess outstanding qualifications. Education equivalent to high school graduation will be an essential requirement. Full details as to conditions governing application and appointment will be announced by the civil service commission shortly, but without going into these matters in detail I may add that applicants who are taken on training and complete their work will qualify for appointment as inspectors either grade II or grade I, depending on their rating as trainees. In British Columbia there are sixteen grade II posts to be filled and nineteen grade I positions. On the east coast there are, in New

Brunswick, fourteen grade II and nineteen grade I posts to be filled; in Nova Scotia, seventeen grade II and ten grade I, and in Prince Edward Island, four grade II and one grade I, or thirty-five grade II and thirty [DOT] grade I on the east coast.
As stated before, there will be, in all, thirty-five new inspectorships for British Columbia and sixty-five for the maritimes.
In order to fill these appointments, forty-four candidates in British Columbia and ninety-three in the maritimes will be selected by the civil service commission. The commission will make the selection by "screening" all applications, thus determining by an evaluation of the information the applicants give regarding themselves in their application papers, by interviews and by oral tests, if necessary, w'hat men are best suited to be taken on as trainees. For about the first month of their probationary training period, which will cover something like five months in all, the trainees will be employed in the field as temporary fishery guardians with pay, working under the supervision of some of our present inspectors. Those of them whose work as guardians has indicated that they have an aptitude for fisheries service will then attend a fishery course; for those on the west coast, in the Vancouver area, and, for those on the east coast; probably at Windsor, Nova Scotia. This course will be carried on jointly by fisheries, veterans affairs and labour's vocational training section, and will include a study of such subjects as methods of fish processing and inspection, fisheries biology, and so on, as well as instruction in the duties of fisheries inspectors. During the course the men will receive the basic grants provided under the vocational and educational training plan for veterans, together with the monthly allowances for dependent children. At the end of the course the candidates will be rated on their work, and those who have reached the required standing will be given an oral examination. The course record and the showing made in the oral test will together determine the candidate's final rating. In the maritimes there are, in addition to the new inspectorships, a number of permanent seasonal vacancies which offer employment for from seven to eleven months of the year. Should qualified eligible candidates remain after the full-time positions have been filled, they may be offered seasonal positions.
The established preference for ex-servicemen with overseas service will apply in case of appointments. In addition, preference in appointments will be given, first, to qualified

Supply-Fisheries
residents of the fisheries sub-district in which the vacancy occurs and, second, to qualified residents of the province concerned.
That briefly outlines the present plans for the expansion and improvement of the outside service of the department, and it is expected that all the 100 new inspectors will have completed their training, be appointed and on the job by May 1, 1947. I sincerely hope that, with the training these new inspectors receive, they will prove themselves to be educationists and not mere police officers. I want them to be regarded as friends of the fishermen. I also hope and trust that these plans will meet with the approval of this committee and of the industry as a whole. I further hope that these new younger men in the service will eventually provide, by way of future promotion, many suitable administrative officials for this department in the years to come. I am firmly convinced that the best way to obtain suitable officials is by way of promotion within the service, provided that they have had the proper groundwork and training; and that proper groundwork and training should be in the early years of their employment and in the outside field service of the department.
I am not as yet in a position to make any announcement as regards the reorganization and expansion of the inside service of the department, but I hope it will not be long before I shall be able to do so. I have adopted the policy of reorganizing from the bottom to the top instead of vice versa. By adopting these present plans for reorganization, I hope that in the future, whoever may be minister of fisheries, will not find himself in the position in which I have found myself, in that there is an inadequate number of suitable officials in the department. In saying this, I am not casting any reflections on my predecessors in office, because it must be borne in mind that we had those years of depression when every effort was made to cut expenditures to a minimum, followed by the war years when this department had to be neglected by reason of the prosecution of the war. Nor am I casting any reflection on the officials of this department, I can frankly say that, on the whole, the Department of Fisheries has able, competent and suitable officials, but the one big drawback is that there are not enough of them. To-day we have several senior officials either going out on pension or soon to go out, and we have not, in some instances, suitable men in the department to be promoted to take their places. The officials that we have are good and competent; but, as I have said before, there are not enough
of them. I wish to take this opportunity of paying special tribute to them. I am not going to mention any names. They have given loyal and efficient service to the government of Canada. Many have been overworked and have had to work over a period of years with few or no holidays. This is definitely not a good situation.' With the coming reorganization of the inside service, I hope that I shall be able to improve that situation.
With these remarks regarding the reorganization and expansion of the department, I submit these estimates for the consideration of this committee.

May I, first of all, compliment the minister on the statement he has just made. Those of us who have been interested in fisheries for any considerable number of years have long recognized the fact that, if there was any one department that required new blood in the way of officials and experts, it was the Department of Fisheries. But the need for these officials and experts did not merely arise during the war period. It was evident, to me at least, that steps of this kind should have been taken in the pre-war years. However, I trust that the matter will turn out as the minister expects it will, and personally I have no doubt that the step taken is one which will redound to the benefit not only of the department but of the country and fishing industry as well.
The matter I have to deal with is one on which I would not at this time delay the committee, but it has to do with important questions that are more than national. It has to do writh international affairs and therefore, in my opinion, it cannot wait. It has relation to the policy of four countries oujtside Canada, and I trust that the committee will be a little lenient with me if I do something that I have not been in the habit of doing, namely', to follow my notes closely.
Prior to the commencement of the session,
I placed on the order paper a resolution drawing attention to the danger and possible destruction of Canada's offshore fisheries. Unfortunately, however, no opportunity was afforded to discuss this resolution, so that I am taking this opportunity to bring the matter to the attention of the government in the hope that some action will be taken along the lines I am about to suggest.
May I say at the outset that the matter, although it has to do with fisheries, comes, in the first instance, under the Department of External Affairs. But since the Minister of Fisheries is the minister in the government representing that portfolio, it is his duty, I
Supply-Fisheries

believe, to take the matters I am about to lay before the committee and place them before the government for action.
The question of fishing in offshore areas of the sea, that is, fisheries outside the narrow belt of waters around our shores known as the three-mile limit, is a question which has perplexed many nations since early days. Time will not permit me on this occasion to deal with the history of the rights of nations on the high seas. Suffice it for me to say, however, that, contrary to popular belief, the three-mile limit of jurisdiction is not an accepted international law by any manner of means. Important maritime countries such as Norway, Sweden, Russia, Italy, Portugal and others have never recognized, and do not at the present time recognize or admit the principle of a three-mile limit of jurisdiction.
While it is true that Great Britain and the United States, on the other hand, have generally adhered to the three-mile limit, nevertheless both these countries have on many occasions changed the limit to suit some special occasion. In 1926 the league of nations sent a draft agreement regarding this matter to almost all the nations, the replies to which are most interesting. Norway claimed rights over ten marine miles, a limit which, by the way, that country has maintained for over two hundred years. The Swedish government claimed rights to four miles; Portugal claimed rights to twelve marine miles, and Portugal also stated in her reply that it was absolutely necessary for that country to preserve the species of fish which inhabit her waters, pointing out that, if those species became depleted or disappeared, Portugal's economic position would be endangered.
Canada's position in regard to her fisheries is similar to that of Portugal. The Spanish government has long adopted jurisdiction over territorial waters for six miles out from her shores. Russia has extended and claims sea control for a distance of twelve miles from all her coasts bordering on the ocean. It is not generally known that on September 16, 1821 the Emperor Alexander issued an order in which the whole west coast of America north of the fifty-first parallel was declared to belong exclusively to Russia, foreign ships being prohibited from approaching within 100 Italian miles off the North American Pacific shores under penalty of confiscation.
Although most countries replied to the draft agreement of the league of nations, it is interesting to note that the British government made no statement whatsoever on the matter. The silence of Great Britain and other governments of the British empire is signi-

ficant and would seem to indicate at least some recognition that the three-mile limit is becoming obsolete in view of present-day conditions. As already mentioned, and as could be proved if time permitted, there is no international law designating three miles as the limit of jurisdiction off our shores. Down through the ages the nations have at various times taken jurisdictional powers on the high seas and for greater distances than the distance ancient cannon were able to fire, which in those days was not more than three miles.
I want now particularly to deal with the reasons why I believe it is important and imperative that Canada take steps to control the waters off her shores so as to protect from possible exploitation and destruction our great fisheries. First of all, may I say that few countries are so fortunate as Canada in having their fisheries at their own back door, so to speak. Most nations have to travel far afield for fish supplies or catches.
Many foolishly believe that the fish in the sea or in the ocean are inexhaustible. Such, however, is not the case. It has been incontestably proved that some of the most valuable coastal and ocean fisheries are susceptible to depletion by overfishing, even though such fishing may be carried on more than three miles from shore. The great banks on the Atlantic are proof alone of this statement. The North sea and the Arctic ocean, as well as the great banks of Newfoundland and Labrador, draw the fleets of more than a score of nations.
Canada, however, especially on the Pacific coast, can obtain her supplies of fish within short sailing distances of her shores. The great Canadian fisheries are either in inside waters or offshore within safe distance of our harbours. Canada so far, however, has paid little attention, if any, to fishing on the high seas either on the Atlantic or on the Pacific. The Canadian government has made no effort whatsoever to define Canadian fishermen's offshore limits if they should be challenged by another nation, except in a treaty with the United States covering halibut; nor, so far as I know, has the government disclosed its reaction or intention in regard to the proposal of protective conservation zones in offshore waters made recently by the President of the United States.
As a matter of fact, the Canadian government has scarcely lifted a finger to survey and explore the riches of our offshore fishing grounds in which every nation at the present time could fish with impunity and to the destruction of these fisheries. Whilst what I have to say applies to Atlantic as well as
AUGUST 28, 194t>
Supply-Fisheries
Pacific waters, I want to emphasize the problem from the Pacific outlook, owing to the fact that I am more familiar with the Pacific than with the Atlantic.
The Pacific deep sea fisheries, like those of the Atlantic, are extremely important to Canada and her economy. Canadian fishermen in these offshore waters fish side by side with fishermen of the United States not only for halibut but for pilchard, herring, salmon, cod, tuna, sardines and many other types of fish as well.
It is obvious that at the present time no regulation or limitation can or should be placed upon Canadian vessels fishing outside the three-mile limit, unless similar limitations are enforced upon vessels of the United States fleet. Whilst it is true that the United States fishing fleet has taken the cream of the fisheries, from waters off the Canadian coast, the greatest danger tc our Pacific fisheries, as well as to our Atlantic fisheries in the future, is from the danger of exploitation by nations other than the United States. Take the case of but one variety alone, that of our salmon.
Here is an industry which gives employment to many thousands of our citizens, and one in which many millions of dollars are invested. All the salmon caught either in offshore waters or inshore waters or in our rivers and lakes are all salmon which have been born and reared in Canadian or United States streams and lakes. Where it not for the fact that Canada, and the United States as well, have enacted conservation measures to protect these fish, there would be no salmon fishery on the Atlantic or the Pacific to-day. The importance of the Canadian fishing industry to our economy is shown by the following statistics:
The total marketed value of all
fish in 1945	 $100 million
Total capital invested	 G7 million
Total numbers employed	 81,000
However, this is but part of the story. To preserve this industry, Canada has spent over $122 million in the protection, conservation and rehabilitation of the fisheries on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts.
Bear in mind, Mr. Chairman, that Canadian rivers and lakes provide the home and nursery beds for all species of salmon. After hatching, the salmon remains from six to eighteen months in the lakes and streams and then goes out to sea. Included in the many salmon streams and rivers we have in Canada is the greatest salmon producing river in the world, namely, the Fraser. Quite a few years ago Canada entered into a treaty with the United States regarding both coasts and with the state
of Washington and British Columbia. Over the entire length of both coast lines there runs an undershelf known as the continental shelf. In some places the water over the shelf of rock is not over a hundred feet in depth. It is to this shelf of rock on the Pacific and the Atlantic that the salmon go and play around until they reach maturity. In the second, third and fourth year, depending on the species and variety of salmon, when fully grown to maturity they return to lay their eggs on the gravel bars of Canadian rivers and lakes whence they came.
Here is the danger. While the fish are playing around in these shallow waters, any country other than the United States and Canada can send fleets of boats to where the salmon are and, by intense fishing, entirely wipe them out. Is Canada, therefore, going to stand idly by while this happens, or shall we be sensible and join with the United States in designating these waters as ours for fishing? Canada and the United States have a just and prior claim to these fish, even though they are out in the open sea, because, but for Canada and the United States, there might not be any salmon there at all, because we provide the home and nursery for them. On the other hand, we not only regulate and control our own fishermen in order to preserve and perpetuate the fish, but we have also expended considerable sums of money in doing so.
The United States is much more alert to the dangers threatening her offshore fisheries than we in Canada seem to be, and therefore is taking action to avoid disaster. As recently as September last, President Truman announced that the United States government had decided to regulate and control fisheries on the high seas contiguous to United States territory. The order by President Truman provides for establishment, under recommendation of the secretary of the interior and the state department, of conservation zones in areas of the high seas contiguous to United States coasts. Until this order was passed, the only sea fisheries which the United States had participated in regulating were those of whales, pacific halibut and fur seals. The new order by President Truman notifies other nations that in areas where fisheries have been, or hereafter shall be developed and maintained by nationals of United States alone, bounded zones will be set up in which United States may regulate and control all fishing activities. This new policy announced by the president will enable the United States to protect effectively at least one of its most valuable Pacific fisheries, that of the Alaska salmon. As the President stated in his proclamation, uncontrolled
Supply-Fisheries

fishery activities and fisheries which allow foreign nations to fish with no thought of conservation, have constituted an ever-increasing menace to the salmon fishery of the United States, and therefore, he declares, to United States welfare.
Canada's position is similar to that of the United States. An underwater shelf of rock similar to that of the continental shelf on the Pacific runs parallel to the Atlantic coasts of the United States and Canada, and it is my information that the United States are considering taking steps also to protect those outside shallow waters on the Atlantic from exploitation by foreign fishing vessels.
The bill introduced by the President goes much farther than this, however, in that an invitation is made to other countries to join with him in this important measure. It is intended that, in areas where the nationals of other countries may be involved, zones will be established by agreements, and joint regulations will be made effective.
Here, Mr. Chairman, I would ask per* mission of the committee to place on record the proclamation of the President of the United States rather than take the time to read it.

(The proclamation is as follows:)
Policy of the United States With Respect to
Coastal Fisheries in Certain Areas of the High Seas
By the President of the United States of America
A Proclamation
Whereas for some years the government of the United States of America has viewed with concern the inadequacy of present arrangements for the protection and perpetuation of the fishery resources contiguous to its coasts, and in view of the potentially disturbing effect of this [DOT] situation, has carefully studied the possibility of improving the jurisdictional basis for conservation measures and international cooperation in this field; and
Whereas such fishery resources have a special importance to coastal communities as a source of livelihood and to the nation as a food and industrial resource; and
Whereas the progressive development of new methods and techniques contributes to intensified fishing over wide sea areas and in certain eases seriously threatens fisheries with depletion ; and
Whereas there is an urgent need to protect coastal fishery resources from destructive exploitation, having due regard to conditions peculiar to each region and situation and to the special rights and equities of the coastal state and of any other state which may have established a legitimate interest therein;
Now. therefore, I. Harry S. Truman, President of the United States of America, do hereby

proclaim the following policy of the United States of America with respect to coastal fisheries in certain areas of the high seas:
In view of the pressing need for conservation and protection of fishery resources, the government of the United States regards it as proper to establish conservation zones in those areas of the high seas contiguous to the coasts of the United States wherein fishing activities have been or in the future may be developed and maintained on a substantial scale. Where such activities have been or shall hereafter be developed and maintained by its nationals alone, the United States regards it as proper to establish explicitly bounded conservation zones in which fishing activities shall be subject to the regulation and control of the United States. Where such activities have been or shall hereafter be legitimately developed and maintained jointly by nationals of the United States and nationals of other states, explicity bounded conservation zones may be established under agreements between the United States and such other states; and all fishing activities in such zones shall be subject to regulation and control as provided in such agreements. The right of any state to establish conservation zones off its shores and in accordance with the above principles is conceded, provided that corresponding recognition is given to any fishing interests of nationals of the United States which may exist in such areas. The character as high seas of the areas in which such conservation zones are established and the right to their free and unimpeded navigation are in no way thus affected.
Executive Order
Providing For the Establishment of Fishery Conservation Zones
By virtue of and pursuant to the authority vested in me as President of the United States, it is hereby ordered that the Secretary of State and and Secretary of the Interior shall from time to time jointly recommend the estab-lismment by Executive orders of fishery conservation zones in areas of the high seas contiguous to the coasts of the United States, pursuant to the proclamation entitled "Policy of the United States with Respect to Coastal Fisheries in Certain Areas of the High Seas," this day signed by me, and said Secretaries shall in each case recommend provisions to be incorporated in such orders relating to the administration, regulation and control of the fishery resources of and fishing activities in such zones, pursuant to authority of law heretofore or hereafter provided.
Harry S. Truman.
The White House September 28, 1945
