(The proclamation is as follows:)
Proclamation of the President of the Republic of Mexico
The President Recovers, in the Name of the Nation, our Submarine Continental Territory Control of Fisheries Resources in the High Seas Present and Future Conservation of Incalculable Natural Riches Which Clearly Constitute Part of the Natural Resources The Executive Recommends the Carrying out of the Bills for the Establishment of Pertinent Law-the Submarine Bed Adjacent to the Coastline Out to 200 Meters Below the Surface is to Belong to Mexico The President of the Republic issued yesterday an order of historic importance in accordance with which the national territory of our nation is to extend to include dominion over all the platform or submarine continental shelf adjacent to our shores provided it not be in excess of a depth of 200 meters with a view to preserving all the natural known or unknown riches that may be found in the seabed, such as mineral products, fauna and flora. Particular pains will be taken for vigilance, use and control of zones of fisheries protection with a view to seeking the development of the resources of the high seas irrespective of the distance separating them from the coastline.
The Chief of the Nation in taking this exceedingly important step announces that he is already giving appropriate orders so that the authorities who have jurisdiction over this new thesis of Mexican territory may proceed to form the appropriate projects of law and the fulfillment of those treaties which may be necessary.
The experience of recent years has shown the increasing necessity for state to preserve those natural riches which throughout the years for various reasons have been beyond their control and beyond integrated development.
As is known, the lands constituting the continental masses in general do not rise in steep slope from the great depths of the ocean but rather rest upon a submarine foundation termed continental shelf which is limited by a line joining points of equal depth (200 meters) from which the slope descends either suddenly or gradually into the zones of middle depth of the seas. Obviously, therefore, this platform or shelf constitutes an integral part of continental countries and it is neither reasonable, nor wise, nor possible that Mexico shall fail to take care of jurisdiction, development, and control of this shelf in those areas adjoining its territory in both oceans.
It is now known, as a result of various scientific investigations, that in this continental shelf there are natural riches, minerals, liquids and gases, phosphates, calcium, hydrocarbons, etc., of an incalculable value contained in the submarine platform the legal incorporation of which to the national territory is necessary and not to be deferred.
On the other hand it is equally urgent that the Mexican nation, which nature has endowed with fisheries resources of an extraordinary
wealth, such as those which are to be found, not to mention others, in the maritime area off Lower California, protect, exploit, and develop these resources in an orderly fashion. This matter is the more urgent today when the world impoverished and needy through the war brought about by totalitarianism, must increase to the maximum its food production.
In the years before the war the western hemisphere had to watch permanent fleets of non-continental countries dedicating themselves to immoderate and exhaustive exploitation of these great resources which, while it is true must help in the welfare of peoples, obviously belong first to that country which possessed them and to that continent to which they belong. Because of its very nature, it is necessary that this protection be carried as far out as those places or zones indicated by science for the development of the fisheries resources of the high seas irrespective of the distance separating them from the coast.
Basing its action upon these reasons, the government of the Republic recovers all the platform or continental shelf adjacent to its coastline and every and each natural resource, whether known or unknown, found therein, and is moving toward that vigilance, use, and control in the zones of fisheries protection necessary to the conservation of such a source of well being.
The above does not imply that the government of Mexico intends to fail to recognize legitimate rights of third parties on a basis of reciprocity or that the government of Mexico intends to affect legitimate rights of free navigation on the high seas since the only thing it seeks is the conservation of these resources for the national, the continental, and world well being.
The government is already issuing orders to the appropriate authorities so that the latter may take steps to formulate the projects of law which are necessary and to negotiate those treaties which may be required.
Manuel Avila Camacho
The President of the Republic.
Mexico, D.F.
October 29, 1945

The action of both these countries, particularly that of the United' States, is of such importance that Canada cannot very well ignore what has been done, and I intend to show, before concluding, that for the future peace of the world, as well as for Canada's own future economy, we should without delay accept President Truman's offer.
For a moment or two, let us first look at the Pacific halibut fishery. It is not generally known that more halibut is produced from off the Canadian and United States shores than in any other ocean or area of water in the world. Of the total world production of halibut, sixty-six per cent is produced by United States and Canadian fishermen in the Pacific right off our shores. Here is a fishery which, but for the regulatory measures taken by the United States and Canada, might today be largely non-existent. In the early years of halibut fishing, all fishing was done

Supply-Fisheries

comparatively close to shore. We had not at that time developed the diesel engine. Nevertheless. without regulation, this fishery, owing to over-fishing, commenced a rapid decline after the year 1911. In that year the catch of halibut reached a total of 56.9 million pounds. In 1930 this had gone down to 22.6 million pounds.
The Pacific halibut has always been exclusively a United States and Canadian activity. Employed in that industry in 1941 were 576 fishing boats, 173 of these being Canadian. The gross earnings of the Canadian fishermen in 1941 were well over SI million, which makes this industry both for Americans and Canadians an extremely important means of livelihood for great numbers of citizens. Fifty per cent of all halibut caught are now taken in area 2 in the open waters off British Columbia shores. The halibut fishery banks are divided into three areas by the international halibut commission, one of these areas being in the gulf of Alaska and some seventy-five miles or more offshore.
Do not let us forget that, before the war, the United States had considerable trouble with the Japanese in regard to fishing in Alaskan waters, and so serious was it at one time that there was almost open warfare. Prior to the. war, the Japanese had been for years in the habit of sending out large ships on extended investigational and fishing trips to various parts of the world. These ships are known as mother ships and able to go a long way from their home port, for a year at least, without the necessity of returning for supplies. Japan claimed she was merely testing the salinity and the temperature of the sea *water in Alaskan waters but admitted, when pressed, they were fishing for crabs as well. Japan denied most emphatically she was catching salmon. When it was reported to Washington that the real purpose of Japan was to engage in salmon fishing, as well as at the same time mapping out the Alaska coast for military purposes, the authorities at Washington refused to believe such statements. The fishermen of Alaska, however, were able to procure the services of a plane which flew a number of times over these mother ships, and by taking actual photographs were able to show that the Japanese were deliberately lying, and were actually fishing for salmon and using nets between three to four miles in length. It was only when the American fishermen of Alaska, however, threatened to take direct action themselves, that Washington officially protested to the Japanese government, and so Japan had the mother ships withdrawn. Bear in mind that Japan was not then quite ready
[Mr. Re*H..J
for war. It is a well known fact, however, that, had war on the Pacific not intervened, these mother ships from Japan would have increased fishing operations there. They would later have moved down the Alaskan and Canadian coasts, and by the use of their intensive fishing methods and three to four mile long nets destroyed not only the halibut banks, but the salmon and other fisheries off our coast as well. It is to prevent this kind of exploitation and destruction from taking place in the future that President Truman has issued the recent proclamation with the view of extending control over all these offshore fisheries in the Pacific and Atlantic, and inviting Canada or any other country to join with them in the matter of control and conservation.
For the future peace of the world, now is the proper time to join with the United States in designating these offshore areas as areas in which Canada and the United States have distinct claims and justifiable priority rights.
No country can dispute the fact that all varieties of salmon frequenting the continental shelf in offshore Canadian waters have been born and reared under protective and conservative measures in Canadian rivers and lakes. No country can dispute the fact also that the halibut and salmon banks would be largely non-existent were it not for the regulatory and conservation measures enforced by Canada and the United States under mutual agreement, and carried out under an international treaty between the two countries. Let us boldly face the fact that other nations, with no thought or consideration for conservation, may desire to invade these offshore north Pacific fisheries.
The total world production of fish and fishing products in 1940 was around 40,000 million pounds. Of this quantity Japan, prior to the war, produced twenty-two percent of the world's total fisheries production. The United States came second with eleven per cent, and the Soviet Union produced ten per cent, while Canada came tenth on the list with our share amounting to only 3-3 per cent.
Recent reports from Tokyo indicate a systematic campaign by the Japanese government and fisheries officials to break out of the fisheries areas assigned to Japan since their surrender, and with a view to Japan's gradually regaining something of their former dominant fishing empire.
Just what part the Soviet Union will take in the fishing areas of the Pacific formerly controlled by Japan is something which has not yet been made clear. In all likelihood, Russia will take back from Japan the fishing rights and areas around Kamchatka, which

Supply-Fisheries
fishing rights, as we know, were forced from Russia following the Russo-Japanese war of 1911.
Information has only recently come from Moscow that Russia has set up two distinct ministries of fisheries, one for the Black and Caspian seas areas, and the other for the northern Pacific. Before that country gets time to become wholly equipped for fishing or before Japan once again sails the seas of the world with her large mother ships, notification should be served on the world by Canada in conjunction with the United States of the justifiable rights and protective interests both countries have in these important fisheries off the British Columbia and Alaskan coasts. By doing so now, all countries will know in advance what our claims are and the reasons for our claims in these areas and will, I believe, be reluctant, in the face of these justifiably claimed rights, to invade the designated fishing areas. Action of this kind by Canada and the United States may be one practical way of keeping peace and preventing war. It will certainly be much more difficult in the future, if action of this kind is not taken, to remove fishing vessels belonging to other nations, if they invade these fisheries, and who might have no hesitation in sending vessels to fish in these areas, we're no such protective regulations in existence.
Three countries, Russia, the United States and Canada, have an equal stake in the potentialities of the north Pacific fisheries, and a vital interest in how modern mechanized methods of fishing will affect the fishery of their respective territorial waters. All the salmon found in the north Pacific ocean propagate in the rivers flowing into the north Pacific from the hinterland of Russia, Alaska, British Columbia, Washington and Oregon.
Following an agreement being reached between Canada and the United States regarding regulatory and protective measures on the fishery off United States and Canadian territory, a further step could then be taken jointly by both governments looking toward the pooling of all the scientific information now available within all three countries, and with the further object of the establishment of an international commission, through which to assess all the facts upon which regulations should be based. The examples of the international halibut commission and the international Pacific salmon commission, both of which are under the joint control of the United States and Canada, places us in a 63260-348J
position to make a valuable contribution to the greater objective, embracing the fisheries of the entire North Pacific.
Here is a further opportunity for Canada to show leadership in world affairs, by first joining with the United States along the lines contained in the recent proclamation and then later moving forward conjointly with the United States in friendly discussions with Russia, and invite that country to join with the United States and Canada in any protective measures deemed desirable for the development of the fisheries in north Pacific waters, in, which all three countries have special interests.
It has been stated that one of the difficulties which might confront Canada, were we to accept the invitation outlined in President Truman's proclamation, has to do with the fisheries on the Atlantic. Whilst this may or may not be correct, it will be most unfortunate if we close our eyes to the situation, and nothing is done by Canada, owing perhaps to some seeming difficulties, which certain high officials at Ottawa think may arise, regarding any protective regulation of fisheries off the Canadian or Atlantic coast.
In the past, Canada has been far too reluctant to protect her own interests where other countries were involved. Two striking instances of the truth of this statement have occurred on the Pacific coast. By our negligence we lost all the rights on the Columbia river given to Canada under a treaty with the United States in 1845. So far as I can find out, no protest was ever made by Canada against the loss of these rights.
I have brought this matter before the house on two occasions, under Prime Minister Bennett and under the present Prime Minister. The only answer I could get was that I had introduced a matter of a delicate nature affecting another nation. But we had rights; we were given rights in 1845, under a treaty. I shall not take time to read the treaty, but as Canadians we had rights of sailing from the interior of British Columbia right to the Pacific coast. But we sat quietly by and allowed the Americans to close up the entire river by the construction of large dams.
Another case I have in mind, where Canada has been derelict in her duty to defend her rights, is that on the coastal waters known as Hecate strait between the mainland of British Columbia and Queen Charlotte islands. Here is a stretch of water, which is strictly Canadian waters and was so regarded by Canada up until at least the year 1907. However, for quite a number of years past United States fishing vessels have been fishing with impunity in these Canadian waters, and without objection or protest by Crnada. Prior to 1907,
Suppl v-Fish eries

United States fishing vessels had attempted to fish in Hecate strait, but on every such occasion instructions were given by the Canadian government to the Canadian fisheries patrol service to chase them off and prevent what was then termed illegal fishing.
Back in 1905 the government of that day set up a commission to investigate all fishing matters on the Pacific coast. One of the particular matters investigated by the commission was that of Hecate strait, and a report of their recommendation was made in 1907.
While it is not my intention to quote the entire recommendations, I shall quote an excerpt from them, because I believe it is necessary that I do so at this time. I quote from page 29 of the Report and Recommendations of the British Columbia Fisheries Commission, 1905-1907, where it states:
This strait has always been regarded as British Columbian waters, and no fishing operations by parties not British subjects were carried on there until about fifteen years ago. As soon as it was realized that the halibut banks between Queen Charlotte islands and the mainland coast were being marauded by foreign vessels, an order was issued by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries at the time, warning all fishing vessels, not flying the British flag, out of these waters. The wire conveying these instructions to the officer in command of the dominion cruiser Quadra is dated April .18, 1896.
I am going to read only one or two further excerpts from these recommendations. I would say, however, that they deal with the matter completely. The recommendation to the government was that these waters were strictly Canadian, and they said that no other fishing ships should be allowed to fish there. The report states further:
The waters are territorial Canadian waters, from which United States and other foreign fishing vessels are legally excluded.
And again:
In these waters occur the most valuable halibut and salmon resorts in the world, and no measures should be neglected to preserve them, and to prevent their threatened depletion by foreign poachers.
That was the last that was heard of the report. The Canadian government just shut their eyes or went to sleep in the matter, and appeared to be afraid, although right along, up to that time, they had been asserting that these waters were our waters. As I say, Canada has, since then, simply closed her eyes to the entire matter.
Action should certainly be taken by the Canadian government to clear up the matter as speedily as' possible, making clear to the United States and to other nations that Hecate strait is, without any peradventure of doubt, Canadian waters and entirely under
fMr. Reid.]
the jurisdiction and control of the Canadian government. I quite realize there may be difficulties now that Canada has entered into a treaty with the United States in regard to the regulation of halibut fishing in Hecate strait and in the gulf of Alaska. In view of this treaty, I am not suggesting that steps be taken now to chase the Americans off these waters. I am suggesting, however, that we should make it clear to the United States that, although we have entered into a treaty with them to preserve and control halibut fishing in the waters of the British Columbia and Alaskan coast, this does not give them any vested right of law, to fish with impunity in Hecate strait.
In Alaskan waters, the United States had no compunction back in 1924 in chasing a Canadian fishing boat in Clarence strait out of there, and later fining the owners for fishing illegally in those waters, even though the Canadian vessel was twenty miles off shore.
One way out of the difficulty with the United States in regard to Hecate strait would be for Canada to take the advantage offered us in President Truman's proclamation, In coming to an agreement with the United States to act conjointly in protecting the fisheries on the continental shelf off the United States and British Columbia coasts, we could come to some agreement with the United States regarding these waters. Such an agreement wiould strengthen Canada's position in the event of any attempted future exploitation by fishing vessels belonging to other foreign nations. In doing so, however, Canada should take a firm stand that the waters of Hecate strait are entirely and strictly Canadian waters. A further advantage in taking action of this kind now would be to deter, in the future, Japanese, Russian or citizens of any other country from fishing there. As the matter stands at present, there is nothing to hinder any country from sending vessels to fish there and in any protests or representations made by Canada against such exploitation, our position in the matter would be weakened owing to the fact that we have allowed the United States to fish there without protest and have not officially declared Hecate strait to be Canadian territory.
I urge the government that now is the opportune time for Canada to take action similar to that of the United States and the republic of Mexico. By so doing, it would indicate to the world that the governments of the three countries were in entire agreement on the matter, and that any exploitation by foreign fishing vessels on the continental shelf off the shores of the North American

Supply-Fisheries
continent would be an unfriendly act and an encroachment involving the governments of Mexico, the United States and Canada. It is my belief that an agreement of this kind between the three governments mentioned, especially an agreement with that of the United States, would have a deterrent effect on other countries and thereby help preserve peace.
Before closing, may I mention one further cogent argument in favour of Canada accepting the invitation announced in President Truman's proclamation. Canadian fishermen at the present time fish for tuna and pilchards right off the coasts of Washington and Oregon. They do so side by side with fishing vessels of the United States. When the provisions of President Truman's proclamation are put into effect, the restrictions as to fishing will undoubtedly cover the offshore waters of Washington and Oregon. If no treaty or agreement is entered into with the United States, what will the position of the Canadian fishermen be, especially when one considers that under the proclamation the chief purpose of the United States is to protect for her own nationals the fisheries adjacent to United States territory. President Truman's proclamation, if ignored by Canada, will undoubtedly have the effect of preventing, in the future, Canadian fishermen from fishing in areas preserved solely for United States nationals.
I repeat, no time should be lost by Canada in taking action similar to that of the United States and Mexico. A committee of competent officials and representatives of the entire industry should be set up immediately to explore and examine the entire situation. It cannot be too strongly pointed out that in this matter time is extremely important for us. The world just now is in a state of flux. Japan at the moment, whilst in a strait-jacket, will not always be kept there. Soviet Russia, although having set up a ministry of fisheries for the Pacific, will require time to gather a fishing fleet together and get fully organized. Russia's first move may undoubtedly be the taking over from the Japanese all the Kamchatka fishing rights, which she was forced to relinquish to Japan by the terms of the Portsmouth treaty in 1911.
As I say, now that the United States is taking action to protect her national interests and realizing what might and could occur in the future, there should be no further hesitation or delay on the part of Canada to do likewise. One particularly strong factor, in favour of our doing so, is that we would have the assurance of the backing and support of the United States in whatever conservation and protective measures may be deemed
desirable and necessary to prevent the exploitation, if not destruction, of the valuable fisheries off our shores.
Finally, in urging the government to accept President Truman's offer and in suggesting that Canada join with the United States in measures to protect our offshore fisheries, I quite realize that this may involve some change of policy in external affairs. I say this because, since confederation, Canada has made no foreign commitments involving matters as important as this without first seeking the advice of British authorities. This policy is quite understandable when one considers that we have had to depend on Great Britain for protection should Canada be attacked or become involved in serious difficulties with other countries. We cannot escape the fact, however, that in so far as our offshore fisheries are concerned, our interests are more closely allied with those of the United States, rather than with those of Great Britain. It is my belief that any measures taken by the United States to protect that country's offshore fisheries from exploitation by other countries, such as an invasion, would certainly affect the interests of this country. Canada could not very well in that event remain neutral or silent on such an important issue, for the exploitation of these offshore fisheries would affect the economy of Canada equally with that of the United States.
My chief purpose in appealing to the government at this time is to draw their attention to the grave dangers facing Canada's salmon fisheries, and to urge that we take action now, and before it is too late.

Mr. Chairman, you and this committee must -have appreciated the wonderful ministerial address or outline of his stewardship which the minister gave us to-day, and also the direct plans he has laid out for the benefit of fisheries in Canada. He was followed by the hon. member for New Westminster who gave us one of his classics on the history of fisheries, not only in British Columbia but throughout Canada generally. During the session we have listened to debates on bacon, wheat, milk and so on; I hope we can now make the fish diet as appetizing.
Before we pass on to the estimates, I should like to make a few remarks which may not be quite along the lines of the remarks of the minister or of the hon. member who has just spoken. I desire to make my remarks relative to the fisheries of the maritimes, and to the fisheries of Prince Edward Island particularly. Last year it was my pleasure to congratulate the minister on his appointment to
Supply-Fisheries

the position he now holds. I hoped at that time that, being a maritimer, he would endeavour to give us some special benefits. After hearing what he said to-day, I am in duty bound to say that he has launched a policy which will be of benefit, not only to fisheries in general, but to those of the maritimes as well.
Last session I brought t'o the attention of the minister certain complaints which had been made by the fishermen in my riding. On their behalf I want to thank the minister for agreeing to their requests. They greatly appreciate his doing these things to which I will refer in a moment.
It is important to have a capable deputy in the Department of Fisheries. In the past the department has had capable deputies, one of whom I should like to mention, the late Doctor William Found. He was a Prince Edward Islander. The department was fortunate in securing as his successor another capable deputy, Doctor Finn. I regret that the department has since lost the services of Doctor Finn, at least for the time being. His ability has been recognized abroad, and I understand that almost 100 per cent more valuation has been placed upon his services, so that we could hardly hope to hold him. But if a man is as valuable as that to the fisheries of some other country I would think he would be just as valuable to the fisheries of Canada. We should not let dollars and cents take such a man away from us. I only hope that he will be available to assist at any time that he may be needed by the department.
The appointment of deputies is generally a political matter, but promotions should be in order. The minister has in his department men with excellent practical training, and I should like to mention a few of them. As director of fish culture he has J. A. Rodd; as director of western fisheries he has A. J. Whitmore; as assistant deputy minister he has
D.	H. Sutherland. I could go on and mention a number of others, all of them capable men. When a deputy is being appointed to assist the minister I hope that qualification for the position will be considered more than political affiliation. I feel that the man selected for this high position should be one with practical knowledge and experience gained from a contact with fisheries.
I am afraid that during the last five years of the war the controls which have been imposed have not always been for the benefit of the fishing industry. This was true in the case of the allocations made, and it was certainly true in the matter of price ceilings. For instance, the fish administration of the

wartime prices and trade board made a distinct differentiation between the prices of canned chicken haddock and canned mackerel. Why? I do not know, because it should have been known to the department that there was no difference in the food value, nor was there much difference on the open market before the controls were instituted.
Another matter is the price ceiling which was set on canned shad, in which case the calculations were based on the cost of the raw materials. Then it was found out that, with the development of the industry, competition arose and the industry had to stop this particular variety because the price ceiling prohibited its production. In my opinion this matter should have been immediately investigated and the price ceiling adjusted, so that this fish could have been added to the already needed food supply; and it should have been investigated by the Department of Fisheries.
Another friendly criticism I have to make with reference to departmental affairs is that apparently they carry on those affairs without proper consultation with the industry itself. In case after case they have made regulations which in principle probably are right, but which in detail lack much. Usually it has happened, prior to the war and during the war, that these regulations-
Would the hon. member tell me whether he is referring to regulations made by the wartime prices and trade board or by the department?

The wartime prices and
trade board. They have been dillydallying around, over and over, and they made the regulations law by order in council and sprung them on the industry without its foreknowledge but, almost invariably in the last years, after canning or processing was well under way. The point which must be emphasized is that if these new regulations are to be instituted they must be considered w'ell in advance of the packing season, and proper notice given to the parties concerned so that plans can be made accordingly, and the man who should boss this proceeding is the Minister of Fisheries, not the wartime prices and trade board. The minister should have the final say, and I must add that this year he has had his say; the minister, when making some changes in regulations, did notify the fisheries and the fishermen throughout the maritime provinces and, probably, all over Canada.
Another little item I wish to speak on for a moment relates to the supervisors, similar to

Supply-Fisheries
the men envisaged in the plan which is being put forth at the present time. What the department needs are good practical men as supervisors, men who, besides seeing that all regulations are properly carried out, will promote and improve all matters pertaining to local fishing conditions. We realize that they are not able to make policy or regulations for the department, but we believe that in many cases they are in a position to recommend things which would be beneficial to the industry, if they are capable of seeing these improvements.
Another matter which I should like to draw to the attention of the minister may not affect the maritimes generally as much as it affects Prince Edward Island: I refer to fishing facilities of the nature of navigation aids, wharves, boat harbours and shelters. Much provision of this kind is needed in various places, but I believe that it should only be carried out after the minister has consulted the local committees or the fishermen direct. .1 know that, in the past, engineers of the Department of Public Works have gone to work and put up structures which have been a mere waste of money because they were entirely unsuited to local conditions. Therefore the Department of Fisheries and the Department of Public Works should always get together with the local people to figure out the best possible way to provide satisfactory structures. This might be a little embarrassing to the engineers, but they do not seem to understand where or how to place many of the things that need to be built for the fisheries.
I believe that at present the trend of postwar fish business will be toward frozen products, and with this in view some definite plan might be drawn up to provide proper cold storage facilities at the right places. With this goes the question of transportation. Prince Edward Island is particularly hindered in this respect. I need not elaborate on this because the minister knows of our difficulties. I should, however, like to mention one instance, this last year, where the fishermen were promoting a new industry in Prince Edward Island fishing, namely, the trimming, shooking and marketing of frozen scallops taken from our own waters. The frozen product was to be marketed in central Canada; the buyers had to hold their goods in anything but reliable storage, where they were in anxiety day and night lest the machinery might break down, until such time as a truck load could be assembled, and this in turn was routed via the Canadian National main line at Moncton,
via the Wood Island-Cariboo ferry. We could not entertain for one minute the idea of crossing at Borden because of the tremendous freight and truck charges involved therein. Neither could the C.N.R. express give the fishermen any suitable express service from Charlottetown. Incidentally the fishermen were not always able to get proper facilities on the main line of the C.N.R., and they had to await the dispatch of iced fish cars from Halifax. These had no definite schedule, and we were only given a very few hours' notice that shipments could be dispatched in those cars. Our fishermen intend to improve this industry if possible these coming years, and they certainly must have better handling facilities in order to do this in competition with other areas producing the same kind of fish. This is only one instance, and many other problems will develop as we try to invade the frozen fish market.
I am going to take only a few minutes to bring to the attention of the department the rope supply situation. Probably this has been rectified, but in the spring of 1946 it gave the fishermen a great deal of concern, and I had many letters with regard to it. The shortage of supplies of fishing rope gave supply dealers and fishermen in lobster fishing many headaches last spring, and the condition continues even now and affects the fall season of 1946. I am not placing any blame for this condition upon the minister or his department, but I am firmly convinced that the minister should dictate to the wartime prices and trade board, or their cotton administration, or the director of twine and cordage, instead of these bureaucrats controlling the situation and dictating to him and his department, In the quotas for 1946-I want the minister to understand that I am now dealing with and criticizing the wartime prices and trade board-
Thank you.

-suppliers and distributors were not given any extra quotas to take care of the reestablishment of war veterans in lobster fishing. They had been led to believe that, while priorities were filled for veterans, that would not affect the regular quota for these suppliers or dealers. But the distributors who were desirous of assisting and cooperating with the veterans were placed in a precarious condition. I have on my file letters from large distributors who had considered the case of the veteran, so much so that many old-established civilian accounts did not get their requirements. I want to tell the minister and his department that they should make demand on the wartime prices and1 trade board for a

fairer allocation of rope to the veterans by an extra quota for them. All would have been well if the department had been dealing with this matter entirely themselves. As a matter of fact, some of these veterans who in the spring of 1946. had priorities filed were never taken care of, and some fishermen had to leave their gear on the shore and go to some other occupation. A set policy pertaining to the control and distribution of cordage for fishing purposes should be established in time, and I hope that the minister will not take any instructions from the wartime prices and trade board. He and his department are the ones who can give satisfaction to the fishermen and the dealers. I might say further that the bungles which were so far-reaching might have been investigated, by the department, but I suppose it was a difficult thing to do. May I at first associate myself with the hon. member for New Westminster and the hon. member for Queen's in" saying, on behalf of the Nova Scotia members, that we welcome the statement just brought down by the Minister of Fisheries. It shows a direct and healthy outlook toward the problems facing his department and those facing the fishing interests in Canada. Long-range planning of this type will do much for the fishing industry in years to come. I would also compliment most highly the hon. member for New Westminster on his splendid presentation of a problem that affects the west coast. I have never heard it presented so directly or clearly before, and we in the east have now a much better appreciation of what western fishermen are up against. I would say, too, that I enjoyed listening to the constructive speech of the hon. member for Queens, since it shows some of the problems facing the fishermen of Prince Edward Island.
I should now like to say something about the fishing problems of Nova Scotia. On the west coast there is definitely an international problem involving oriental nations. In Nova Scotia we have an international problem involving European nations. In the light of present-day world affairs, it is natural to be internationally minded, and I think Nova Scotians, by virtue of the fact that they have

seafaring traditions, are probably more internationally minded than the average citizen. They are interested in such matters as the peace conference, UNRR<A and the other international conferences that are taking place to-day. But of more immediate interest and direct concern to the fishermen, in the constituency of Queen's-Lunenburg in particular and Nova Scotia in general, is the international situation arising out of the destruction by trawlers of foreign registry of trawl gear set out by our fishing schooners on Quero bank off the coast of Nova Scotia. Quero bank is known officially on most maps and charts as Banquereau, and is located approximately 115 miles off Canso in a southeasterly direction and approximately 245 miles off Lunenburg.
The Department of Fisheries as well as the Department of External Affairs are fully familiar with the situation. It is acknowledged that it poses a difficult problem so far as prevention and redress are concerned because, in the absence of adequate proof of nationalities, the Canadian government is not in a position to approach the foreign government or governments concerned.
It has been known for several years that in some instances foreign trawlers have interfered with Nova Scotian fishing schooners and there have probably been rare cases when our own trawlers have been at fault. This destruction may or may not be intentional. Basic methods of fishing involved are widely different and isolated accidents are understandable. Nova Scotia schooners fish by setting out on the banks long lengths of line equipped with hooks attached at intervals. These lines thus equipped are called trawls. They are quite long and normally are set out in a radial pattern around the schooners. Trawlers, on the other hand, are mjuch more like conventional steamships. They are larger, usually of steel construction, and their method of operating is to drag a net behind them and scoop up the fish, so that, although the gear of our schooners is well marked by buoys, it is understandable that a trawler could cut through it accidentally in isolated cases.
Our fishermen realize that accidents of this kind can happen and they would like to think that these recurrences are accidental. But one must be broad-minded indeed to accept this view in the face of repeated incidents in clear weather, in broad daylight and despite adequate warnings by the schooners. In fact, Quero bank was so congested recently with foreign trawlers, that our schooners oftentimes found it necessary to go around the bank in order to avoid collisions. The fre-

Supply-Fisheries
quency of these incidents has, of course, increased since the war, because the banks are now safe from enemy craft and foreign nations are turning more to peacetime pursuits.
In May of this year the interference by foreign trawlers was brought to the attention of the government, but at that time the evidence was meagre and the government could not establish the identity of the trawlers concerned. The Canadian Fishermen's Union, which entered the complaints, did not provide this information. Skippers were reasonably sure of the nationalities of the offending trawlers, but presumably they did not have sufficient evidence to satisfy themselves completely and, despite repeated attempts, the government was not able to establish these identities.
It is understood that the foreign trawlers have now returned temporarily to their home ports to discharge their cargoes and to refit; but until they did leave the banks, the situation was becoming considerably worse, and it is likely it will deteriorate further when they return. A number of fishing schooners experienced losses of gear in the early summer, and at the request of the Department of Fisheries their skippers prepared sworn statements for submission to the government. It was hoped that these most recent statements would specify the nationalities of the trawlers, but it is understood that they did not. They did set forth much valuable information and evidence of specific instances of destruction, but in no case did they identify the offending trawlers by nationalities.
Both the Halifax Chronicle and the Halifax Herald have been emphasizing the seriousness of the situation, and the Financial Post of August 3 treated the matter rather fully. This last mentioned paper designated the offending trawlers as being of Spanish, Portuguese and French registry, and in an editorial dated August 16 the Herald said the offenders were Spanish, but I am not aware on what evidence these statements were based. The Financial Post further stated that in one instance a Spanish trawler deliberately swept through the well-marked gear of the schooner Irene Mary, but I understand that in his sworn statement the skipper of this schooner designated the offender only as a "foreign" trawler. The captain of this schooner is a neighbour of mine. As is the case with most fishing skippers, he is not given to exaggeration and, in fact, will tolerate a great deal before entering complaints. Under the circumstances, one can assume that the situation is intolerable. However, it is regretted that, although the nationalities of the offending trawlers appear to be common knowledge locally, and some newspapers are sufficiently sure of themselves to designate nationalities in print, the Department of Fisheries is having difficulty in obtaining this information in sworn statements from authoritative sources.
The department is, of course, aware that there are Spanish, Portuguese, and French trawlers on the banks, but no evidence has been presented which will permit it to associate a particular trawler with a specific act of destruction. The most recent affidavits submitted on August 20 and 22 are much more complete than any submitted prior to that time; but, although they again state in three instances that the trawlers were thought to be Spanish, none of them is specific as to country of registry, and the captain of the schooner Irene Mary, Capt. Leo Corkum, says that he cannot identify the nationality of the trawler that damaged his gear. I understand also that on June 3 an R.C.A.F. plane made a reconnaissance flight over Quero and found that, of twelve foreign trawlers on the bank that day, eight were of Spanish nationality. This situation has developed to the point where the existence of our fishing industry may very well be at stake. It is understood that foreign nations are building trawlers in large quantities. For example, it is reported that France is having thirty trawlers constructed in the United States at the present time, and that these trawlers are larger in size than those used by either Canada or the United States. Portugal is assuming an ambitious trawler programme. There is no doubt that these trawlers will fish on the banks which have always been ours by tradition, and it is greatly feared that these fishing grounds will suffer early depletion, just as the European banks have been depleted. Some international understanding is necessary, but pending a satisfactory understanding our fishermen must have adequate protection.
The nature of the protection presents a real difficulty. It is conceivable that this government can declare its rights to control the coastal waters extending to the edge of the continental shelf, just as the United States has done. In fact such a policy would appear highly desirable. The hon. member for New Westminster covered that situation exceptionally well in his treatment of fishing conditions on the west coast. I may say that we support his views entirely; we feel that there is a great deal of merit in his proposal, and I would recommend that the government consider it seriously. I do not deny that there are problems involved, nevertheless it is one approach
Supply-Fisheries

to the problem which must be considered. Quero bank and other fishing grounds which we have long regarded as our own are well within the limits of the continental shelf. But having declared jurisdiction, it would still be necessary for us to provide adequate control measures to protect our rights, unless there were a workable agreement between the nations desirous of using the banks. The last thing in the world we want is unfriendly relations on these banks. Our fishermen do not want to fish surrounded by protective craft in the numbers that would be required if the foreign trawlers chose to ignore our proclaimed rights. Let us hope that enforcement measures of this kind will never be necessary.
In my opinion, therefore, it is of the utmost importance that this government take whatever action is necessary to satisfy itself of the identity of the offending trawlers, and that it come to understandings with their governments at the earliest possible date so that the rights of our fishermen may receive the consideration to which they are entitled. I was pleased to hear the minister say, in his statement on August 14 as reported in Hansard at page 4816, that the matter is being given further detailed investigation not only by his department but by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
Quite apart from the problem of patrolling the fishing grounds under these extraordinary conditions, it is important that adequate patrols be provided even if fishing conditions are normal.
There are no patrol craft in operation on the banks at the present time. The minister provided this information on August 21 in reply to a question I placed on the order paper. Prior to the war, two patrol craft, Arras and Arleaux, did good work, but they were used for war purposes and are no longer available. The department has acquired another ship, the C.G.S. Cygnus. It is understood that this craft, which was formerly the Melville-a minesweeper of the Bangor type-will be ready for operation within the next week or two. It is a sizable craft, approximately 162 feet long and with a speed of seventeen knots. It is understood that she will carry a crew of twenty-seven. Her function will be primarily to provide protection and general services for our fishermen on the offshore banks. It would appear that consideration should be given to obtaining additional such craft to perform general coast guard duties.
It is the opinion of local fishermen that the services of boats such as C.G.S. Cygnus should be supplemented by craft which could travel at high speed and would be available for inshore work. It would seem to me that motor

torpedo boats would lend themselves ideally for this purpose with a minimum of modification.
The R.C.A.F., the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, Department of Transport and Department of Fisheries all have need for some rescue service, patrol service or other type of service along the coast. It is known that lawbreakers use speedy craft and, in order to cope with them, the departments concerned must also use fast boats. I would suggest, therefore, that the four departments I have just mentioned consolidate their efforts in this field and purchase several high speed craft of the motor torpedo boat or similar type. The combination of the Cygnus type craft and these smaller craft would provide more adequate offshore and inshore coverage.
The inland waterways in my constituency are presenting a problem of increasing magnitude. In the first place, there seems to be some uncertainty as to the present and future division of responsibility between the federal government and the provincial government of Nova Scotia, in this field. It seems to me that the first problem is to establish these responsibilities clearly and beyond any doubt. This clarification would remove uncertainty from the minds of many departmental employees and thus result in greater over-all efficiency. It would result, too, in a programme which, by virtue of being clearly defined, would bo more energetically executed.
There are in my constituency several first-class salmon and trout rivers. They present a major attraction for tourists as well as provide food and revenue for local residents. The condition of these rivers has been allowed to deteriorate to the point where they are losing their attraction for tourists and, if corrective steps are not taken in the very near future, this country will lose a valuable source of revenue.
When one sees the benefits accruing from improvements made to streams and rivers on the west Coast, it becomes apparent that we must insist on prompt action to protect these resources in Nova Scotia. The minister knows that I speak particularly of the Mersey and Medway rivers in Queens county and LaHave river in Lunenburg county. But there are others of which the same can be said. The Department of Fisheries is fully familiar with the circumstances and knows the problems involved. I feel that the department is giving the problems full consideration, but I would urge that action be taken. If, as I intimated before, corrective action is impeded in any way because of uncertainty as to responsibilities between the

Supply-Fisheries
dominion and the province, then I would say that it is most important that this vital matter be clarified without delay.
At this point, may I say that the Minister of Fisheries has at all times shown himself to be most anxious to cooperate. He has always taken a realistic and practical view of any problems I have placed before him, and in no case has he dismissed a reasonable request simply by saying that it was not the policy of his department to do "things of that nature."
Would the hon. member permit a question? Is it his opinion that the provincial government has failed to cooperate with the minister in taking the measures necessary?

I did not say that. I do not care to give a detailed opinion. In brief, I would say, no; I did not mean that at all. I do not know of any case in which the provincial government has not cooperated; but, as hon. members know, where there is any uncertainty as to who is responsible there is always inefficiency.
Does the hon. member mean-
The hon. member must not interrupt the speaker without his consent.
I asked for consent.
What was the question?

I wondered whether the hon. member would tell the committee what were the corrective measures necessary. I am very much interested in his speech, and I am just seeking information as a westerner who does not know anything about the problems.

I should like to proceed, and, if time permits, I shall be glad to hnswer the question after-wards. Is that satisfactory?
I was speaking about the minister. At this particular point I was saying that the minister has shown himself to be willing to try new approaches to problems, and we have every confidence that, so long as he holds the portfolio, our fishing problems will receive every consideration.
Wherever there are shore fishermen, there is also the problem of dredging. Dredging, as such, is a matter for the Department of Public Works, but I mention it here because it is so integrally associated with the lot of inshore fishermen. These men leave their homes around two, three or four o'clock in the early morning; go offshore eight or ten
miles to fish, and come back the same afternoon with their catch. Many times they return with a boatload of fish at low tide and, because of shallow water, they are forced to- lie outside the harbour waiting for the tide to rise. Hon. members can well imagine that this is a precarious and uncomfortable situation in rough weather. There are one or two particularly bad places in my constituency where harbours have become filled up with sand or mud. The Minister of Public Works is fully familiar with them and is sympathetic to the predicament of the fishermen. The trouble is that dredging equipment is limited and, where a heavy programme is on the books, all projects cannot be carried out at the same time. The various jobs must, therefore, be listed in order of urgency. I can assure the committee, however, that when fishermen are lying offshore in a storm with a boatload of fish waiting for the tide to rise so that they can enter the harbour, it is not easy to persuade them that their need for dredging is less urgent than that of some other locality. I would, therefore, impress upon the Minister of Public Works through the Minister of Fisheries that any steps he can take to increase his dredging capacity will be well directed in the interests of the fishermen and the economy of this country.
Before concluding, I would say a few words about the Fisheries Research Board of Canada. As is the case with any organization, the board has its opponents and supporters. Scientific or research bodies seem more likely to be the object of misunderstanding and resulting criticism than almost any other type of agency.
The popular impression of scientists and researchers is that they are long-bearded- mentally if not physically-and that not only do they not have their feet on the ground, but their heads are in the clouds.
This thinking is often applied to a lesser extent to engineers. I recall that, in discussing the research council, an hon. member was concerned about the administrative ability of engineers and asked the minister if a practical businessman would be placed in the capacity of administrator over and above the engineers.
These are misconceptions. There are, of course, dreamers and theorizers in science and engineering just as there are in every other field of endeavour. It cannot be said that all who are not scientists or engineers are necessarily good administrators, and by the same token it must not be assumed that all scientists and engineers are poor administrators.
Supply-Fisheries

Research is normally a slow process. It usually requires long-range planning and a long period of work before results are achieved. It is not the sort of field in which one can approach a researcher and say, "Well, what did you discover to-day?" and expect to get a satisfying answer.
The fisheries research board has produced results since it was formed in 1937, and some of them have been outstanding. It is often criticized for what it has not done; that it has not given full help to industry; that it does not have a practical approach to problems and so on, but in all fairness one should give the board due credit for its achievements.
The annual reports set forth clearly the programme and achievements, and I would imagine that all hon. members are familiar with them. But, in particular it is desired to remind the committee of the work of the board in rehabilitating oyster culture in the maritimes; protecting the lobster industry by laying down policies based on long and arduous statistical studies; and the rehabilitation of shad fishing in the headwaters of the bay of Fundy with resultant increase in catch. It has also found the answer to the toxic condition in clams at certain times of the year in the bay of Fundy and has made the public aware when these clams are safely edible. The Nova Scotia department of health on the 17th August issued an official warning to the public, based on the findings of the research board. Fishermen on the east coast are optimistic that the herring investigation will result in herring being available on a year-round basis, rather than on the seasonal and uncertain basis as at present.
The programme laid down for the west coast will undoubtedly result in benefits in a variety of fields. The Skeena salmon investigation alone is an undertaking of great magnitude and great promise. Judging from the reports, I would imagine that whitefish fishermen on the prairies realize the value this board has been to them. The board has made many other contributions and advances w'hich are clearly set forth in its reports, and it would not seem necessary for me to mention them at this time. But judging by the number of requests the board receives from the fishing industry for assistance in various projects, I would gather that its value to this industry is fully appreciated.
I have no particular reason or desire to defend the fisheries board. As far as I am concerned, it must be capable of standing or falling on its own merits. The board consists of a good cross-section of representatives from industry, government and science. Its terms of reference, as set forth in the Fisheries Re-

search Board Act, appear to me to be sound, and the principle of having an organization established to do research, in the fishing industry is sound.
That there is need for such a board is well indicated by the fact that it has already done much valuable work that would otherwise not have been undertaken either by private industry or any other agency.
In conclusion, I would say that we are keenly interested in the development of foreign markets for fish. The termination of the war has resulted in a decreased demand for our fish abroad and has increased the number of nations competing in the struggle for markets.
Recent action by UNRRA in suggesting that this organization be relieved of some of its obligations to accept large quantities of Canadian fish is an indication of the trend in the European market. New markets must be sought and old ones developed. I would, therefore, strongly urge that the Department of Trade and Commerce, through the Canadian Commercial Corporation and its other facilities, leave no stone unturned in its endeavour to develop foreign demands for our fish.

I shall take only a
moment or two to say a few words about fresh-water fishermen and particularly the Ontario federation of commercial fishermen. This is a newly formed organization which consists of an amalgamation of regional fishermen's associations along the Canadian side of the great lakes and the lake of the Woods. One of its chief purposes is to make scientific and thorough investigations into the habits of useful species of fish in the great lakes, their feeding and spawning habits, with a view to conserving useful species and controlling predatory and useless fish.
I bring this matter up now because the federation feels that the federal department can be of great assistance;, owing to the fact that the waters of the great lakes are international waters. I am particularly interested in the federation because one of its laboratories is situated at Port Dover, in my constituency. Port Dover is the home port of what is reputed to be the largest and best equipped freshwater fishing fleet in the world.
Is that a provincial or federal organization?

It. is all in Ontario, and many of the regulations are provincial. However lake Erie in particular is concerned on account of the international feature, because on that lake there are bordering no less than four states of the United States.

Supply-Fisheries
My main purpose in rising is to express the appreciation of the federation for the cooperation of and the assistance given by the minister and his department. I know the federation is well pleased with the help it has been given, and I am sure that help will continue.

I should like to make only a few remarks at this time about the one department concerning which I have no criticism. I would show my appreciation to the minister for the appointment of Mr. Whitmore, because I believe he will have the confidence of the rank and file of fishermen on the coast.
I would also thank the hon. member for New Westminster for his address this afternoon, in which he dealt with both the national and international aspects of the matter. As it applied to fisheries on the Pacific coast I would say the hon. member's speech was a masterpiece, and I know that in years to come it will be used as a reference.
I would point out, however, that, taken as a whole, our fishing fleet on the coast is not as modern as that of the United States, nor is it as well equipped to compete in fishing operations. I would suggest to the minister that some organization be set up by the department under which loans could be given to fishermen in respect of their floating equipment, on a basis which would compare with loans to industry inland. In this way the fishermen could have modern equipment and be better fitted to compete with other countries.
I would associate myself with what the hon. member for New Westminster said respecting Hecate strait. That is a problem facing the halibut fishermen especially, and I have a keen interest in it because the strait is in my riding.
There is one other small matter which, though small, is important. When I was home last, it was brought to my attention that fishermen, when out on the grounds, operating in their cramped quarters for hours, must depend upon refreshments in the nature of a cup of tea and a piece of bread and butter. The feeling is that the butter ration is not adequate. I do not know whether the ration has been increased since last winter, but they ask that a more adequate supply be allowed, because they depend upon it for quick energy.

At the outset,
may I say I support the views expressed to-day by the hon. member for New Westminster. I heartily endorse everything he has said. I am sorry to say the remarks I am about to make will, I realize, be critical to some extent.
I can assure this committee that what I say will, I feel, be expressing the opinion of ninety per cent or more of the fishermen on the Atlantic coast. I know my remarks may not meet with the approval of the Department of Fisheries; but I am sincere when I state no other industry in Canada has a better outlook for the future, if given proper direction and guidance, than the fishing industry of this great country. I regret I have not had an opportunity of visiting my friends in British Columbia to view at first hand their fishing interests, so that naturally my remarks will be confined to the fisheries of New Brunswick and the other maritime provinces, with which I am more familiar.
This industry has gone a long way in the past twenty years toward producing a better commodity and the chief aim on the Atlantic coast over a great period of years has been to give the fishermen better equipment to work with, better boats in which to work, whereby there is less exposure and much more comfortable accommodation. The great improvement in this respect is readily seen if one visits the fishing villages to-day. Unquestionably this improvement is responsible for a much greater investment by the fishermen, because modern equipment is to-day costly, particularly boats which are costing several thousand dollars. Twenty years ago a boat used for the same purpose would cost a few hundred dollars. The size of the modern boat is much larger and, as I previously stated, in most cases it has all modem conveniences, making the life of a fisherman less hazardous and more desirable. This improved equipment makes it possible for fishermen to go farther afield to carry on their fishing activities; distances that a few years ago would have been prohibitive with the inferior boats, engines and gear that were at their disposal at that time.
Since I did not speak during the budget debate, I should like to take this opportunity of congratulating the Minister of Finance on amending the Income War Tax Act to permit fishermen and farmers to average their incomes for a period of three years moving average. In 1948 all farmers and fishermen who have made returns for 1946 and 1947 will be entitled to average their incomes for the three years and pay their tax on their average earnings at the end of 1948. Since the incomes of these primary producers fluctuate to so great an extent, this amendment will rectify an injustice that has been imposed on these people for several years, and I can assure the Minister of Finance that the proposed change will be greatly appreciated by the people of Charlotte county.

Another matter I wish to deal with is the matter of floor prices. As I have stated before, this is the major problem confronting fishermen to-day. True, they have enjoyed, during the past few years a period of prosperity, which was long overdue. This was greatly appreciated, but the future must be faced, and without some security as to floor prices there is little enthusiasm.
To let the committee have some idea as to how prices paid fishermen fluctuate, I wish to give one illustration. During the months of January, February, March and April of this year, herring scales which are produced by sardine fishermen were sold to the processors in the state of Maine for prices ranging from sixty cents a pound to as high as three dollars a pound. Very recently the several buyers got together, and during the past few weeks the price has been ten cents a pound. Hon. members can readily understand the uncertainty with respect to prices paid these fishermen and the absolute necessity of legislation to rectify this unbearable situation. As has been explained to the committee previously, fishermen are producers of a perishable article that cannot be held indefinitely awaiting better marketing conditions, but on the contrary, it must be disposed of immediately or it will be a total loss. Therefore the fisherman is always at the mercy of the manufacturer.
At the same time, the manufacturer would be utterly helpless without the primary producer, because his great investment in buildings and machinery would be of little value if the fishermen, through adverse conditions, are compelled to leave this industry and seek some other form of employment in which they feel more secure and in which they would receive better protection. I am convinced that these men do not wish to have floor prices established that would be unreasonable or that would in any way inflict hardship upon buyers and manufacturers of their products, since we all realize these manufacturers must compete with similar manufacturers in other parts of the world. Canada is an exporting nation and, in respect of fish, seventy-five per cent or more must be sold in other parts of the world. The greater portion exported would go to the United States which is the market the maritime provinces have enjoyed over a great period of years.
In December, 1945, I brought this matter to the attention of this department, pointing out the deplorable situation the fishing industry would inevitably find itself drifting into unless it was safeguarded and protected by floor prices. At that time I suggested an

international agreement as the solution, owing to our dependence upon United States markets for our products. Since that time, no action has been taken regarding this matter, and there are already signs of declining prices, as was explained in the great decrease in the prices paid for herring scales. It also shows how little control fishermen have of their own business and how rapidly prices can fall without some sort of protection. This matter is of vital importance to all our fishermen to-day and steps should be taken immediately, because it would perhaps be more opportune at the present time than to wait until prices begin to fall. It would be utterly impossible for these fishermen to carry on at the present time with prices that prevailed during the depressions period, on account of the fact that prices which they are obliged to pay to-day for materials and equipment necessary to carry on their work, have greatly increased1, and any major decline in prices paid to producers would be disastrous to the fishing industry.
I trust the department is fully aware of the situation and of the necessity of stabilized prices to all primary producers. The migration of our young men from the maritime provinces to the New England states was brought about by this very condition, because prices paid to primary producers other than during war years have been out of all proportion to prices paid by the consumer. In other words, prices paid by the consumer to retailers did not compare in any way with prices paid to the fishermen. The price spread has always been too great.
If the fisheries department are desirous of assisting this great industry, in no way could their effort be better exemplified or in no way could they please the fishermen of this dominion to a greater degree than by guaranteeing stabilized prices. If a poll could be taken within this industry and the question asked as to what the fisheries department could do that would benefit the greatest number of fishermen, the answer from ninety per cent of the fishermen would be, by establishing floor prices.
Regardless of this fact, nothing has been done in connection with this important matter. It has been brought to the attention of the department on different occasions, but apparently the feeling is that their effort can be put to better advantage, so that they have governed themselves accordingly.
I am of the same opinion to-day as last December and still feel confident that an international agreement can be worked out that would meet with the approval of the canners and fishermen on both sides of the

border, and, as long as I am the member for Charlotte county, I will press the fisheries department for some action.
In 1942 a price ceiling was placed on sardines in the fresh state. This was done by the can-ners in New Brunswick and the state of Maine. The ceiling price was not unreasonable to either the producer or the canner. It has been strictly adhered to by both parties and, to my knowledge, no breach has been made, although during that period since the ceiling price was set we have had times of scarcity and times of plentiful supply. However, regardless of supply, the price has never been broken and has worked out advantageously and beneficially to both parties. During the first great war, in 1918 a ceiling and floor price were placed on sardines with exactly the same effect, although in the previous year, 1917, the price had fluctuated from $10 to $95.
If this regulation of prices is necessary in war time to protect the consumer, why should the same consideration and protection not be given the primary producer at all times to accord him adequate security and encouragement, to enable him to establish his business on a more sound basis in order that he might look to the future with a more optimistic viewpoint?
During the past few years, while conditions were more encouraging in the fishing industry, the fishermen have made large investments, particularly the younger men who, in order to establish themselves in the sardine industry, were obliged to build sardine weirs in deep water and locations which necessitated large expenditures, because the privileges that could be maintained at a more reasonable cost had been secured over a great period of years by the older fishermen and are handed down from one generation to another.
If the price of sardines should fall to prewar levels the fishermen would be obliged to abandon a great proportion of these expensive structures and seek some other form of employment and, if past history repeats itself, you will again see the youth of the maritime provinces migrating to the New England states, not through choice perhaps, but by force of circumstances beyond their control. In fact many investments during this period of prosperity in expensive boats, nets and equipment cannot be maintained or replaced when necessary if prices paid to producers during that same time are reduced to such an extent that, after expenses are paid, the producer cannot make a profit.
I realize that no programme is fruitful if it is merely opposed to something. Successful programmes are those which are constructive and creative. What we need at this critical
juncture is an affirmative demonstration that we have the qualities needed for survival. We must be resourceful and. persistent in seeking ways to meet any emergency that may appear, and be in position to surmount any obstacle that might obstruct our path to higher standards of living. Retaliatory barriers would serve to increase distrust and express lack of cooperation. This would prove fatal, because the only solution to our problem is to have voluntary cooperation, both nationally and internationally. That security depends primarily upon ourselves, since we have the support of practically every primary producer in Canada and have also the authority to administer the cure through the cooperation of the primary producers and government officials in Canada and the United States. The old adage that "an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure" could be applied in this circumstance, because it would appear to be a much more simple matter to have the necessary adjustments made at the present time than to postpone taking any action until such time as prices have started to decline.
These primary producers have no C.I.O. or A.F. of L. to look to for protection and would not wish to exert their authority if such an organization did exist, as long as agreements can be reached through friendly cooperative and intelligent discussion.
I have been given to understand that it would be an enormous task to have adjustments made whereby this protection would include all primary products. During the war the necessary machinery was assembled and put into effect to enforce price control. We all agree, I believe, that a very fine job was done in this country under capable management.
Item stands.
